However, for large tables this defeats the purpose of using a database. Instead, you’ll want to query just the data you need.

title: Working with Databases
text:
SQL (Structured Query Language) is the standard language for working with databases. While we’ll primarily use dbplyr to write dplyr code that gets translated to SQL, understanding SQL basics is valuable. Table 2 maps each SQL clause to the dplyr verb you already know from ?@sec-tidy-data.


The most common SQL operation is SELECT, which retrieves data:

# Run a SQL query directly
sql <- "SELECT mpg, cyl, hp FROM mtcars WHERE mpg > 25"
result <- dbGetQuery(con, sql)
as_tibble(result)

# A tibble: 6 × 3
    mpg   cyl    hp
  <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
1  32.4     4    66
2  30.4     4    52
3  33.9     4    65
4  27.3     4    66
5  26       4    91
6  30.4     4   113





A SQL query follows this general pattern:
SELECT columns
FROM table
WHERE conditions
GROUP BY columns
ORDER BY columns
The clauses must appear in this order, though not all are required.



Table 2: SQL clauses and their dplyr equivalents





Clause
Purpose
dplyr equivalent




SELECT
Choose columns, compute values
select(), mutate()


FROM
Specify the table
The data frame name


WHERE
Filter rows
filter()


GROUP BY
Define groups for aggregation
group_by()


ORDER BY
Sort results
arrange()

title: Working with Databases
text:
dbplyr is a dplyr backend that translates your dplyr code to SQL and runs it on the database. This means you can use familiar tidyverse syntax (?@sec-dplyr) without learning SQL.


Use tbl() to create a reference to a database table:

mtcars_db <- tbl(con, "mtcars")
mtcars_db

# Source:   table<mtcars> [?? x 11]
# Database: DuckDB 1.5.2 [root@Darwin 25.6.0:R 4.6.0/:memory:]
     mpg   cyl  disp    hp  drat    wt  qsec    vs    am  gear  carb
   <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
 1  21       6  160    110  3.9   2.62  16.5     0     1     4     4
 2  21       6  160    110  3.9   2.88  17.0     0     1     4     4
 3  22.8     4  108     93  3.85  2.32  18.6     1     1     4     1
 4  21.4     6  258    110  3.08  3.22  19.4     1     0     3     1
 5  18.7     8  360    175  3.15  3.44  17.0     0     0     3     2
 6  18.1     6  225    105  2.76  3.46  20.2     1     0     3     1
 7  14.3     8  360    245  3.21  3.57  15.8     0     0     3     4
 8  24.4     4  147.    62  3.69  3.19  20       1     0     4     2
 9  22.8     4  141.    95  3.92  3.15  22.9     1     0     4     2
10  19.2     6  168.   123  3.92  3.44  18.3     1     0     4     4
# ℹ more rows


Notice that this doesn’t load the data—it just creates a reference. The data stays in the database.



dbplyr operations are lazy: they build up a query without executing it until you explicitly request the data:

# Build a query (doesn't execute yet)
efficient_cars <- mtcars_db |>
  filter(mpg > 25) |>
  select(mpg, cyl, hp, wt) |>
  arrange(desc(mpg))

# See the generated SQL
efficient_cars |> show_query()

<SQL>
SELECT mpg, cyl, hp, wt
FROM mtcars
WHERE (mpg > 25.0)
ORDER BY mpg DESC





Use collect() to execute the query and bring results into R:

# Execute query and return results to R
efficient_cars |> collect()

# A tibble: 6 × 4
    mpg   cyl    hp    wt
  <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
1  33.9     4    65  1.84
2  32.4     4    66  2.2 
3  30.4     4    52  1.62
4  30.4     4   113  1.51
5  27.3     4    66  1.94
6  26       4    91  2.14








Important



Only collect() what you need! Fetching an entire large table defeats the purpose of using a database. Filter and aggregate in the database first, then collect the summarized results.

title: Working with Databases
Working with Databases
text:
Understanding SQL helps you write better dbplyr code and debug issues.


Table 3 lists the syntax differences that trip people up most often.



Table 3: Syntax differences between R and SQL





Aspect
R/dplyr
SQL




Equality
==
=


Logical AND
&
AND


Logical OR
|
OR


Missing values
NA
NULL


Strings
"text" or 'text'
'text' only


Case sensitivity
Case sensitive
Keywords case insensitive









SQL’s NULL behaves like R’s NA—it’s “contagious” in calculations:

mtcars_db |>
  filter(!is.na(mpg)) |>
  show_query()

<SQL>
SELECT mtcars.*
FROM mtcars
WHERE (NOT((mpg IS NULL)))





Sometimes dbplyr generates subqueries—queries nested inside other queries:

mtcars_db |>
  mutate(mpg_group = if_else(mpg > 20, "high", "low")) |>
  filter(mpg_group == "high") |>
  show_query()

<SQL>
SELECT q01.*
FROM (
  SELECT
    mtcars.*,
    CASE WHEN (mpg > 20.0) THEN 'high' WHEN NOT (mpg > 20.0) THEN 'low' END AS mpg_group
  FROM mtcars
) q01
WHERE (mpg_group = 'high')


The subquery is needed because SQL evaluates WHERE before SELECT, so you can’t filter on a column you’re creating in the same query.

title: Your Computational Toolkit: Installing and Using Editors and IDEs
text:
NoteLearning Objectives



After completing this chapter, you will be able to:

Explain what an editor and an integrated development environment (IDE) do for you, and why a small investment in learning one pays off every day
Install the core software for this course: a Unix shell, R, Python, Quarto, TinyTeX, VS Code, and Positron
Navigate the layout of VS Code and Positron, use the Command Palette and the integrated terminal, and install the extensions we rely on
Choose sensibly among VS Code, Positron, and RStudio for a given task
Keep track of which “side” of a Windows computer you are working on when using WSL
Distinguish Jupyter notebooks from Quarto documents, and know what a Python environment is
Install the compiler toolchain your operating system needs to build R and Python packages from source
Verify that everything is installed correctly and troubleshoot the most common installation problems



In ?@sec-introduction you set up the operating-system level of your computer: a Unix shell on macOS or Linux, or Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL) with Ubuntu on Windows. This chapter fills in the rest of the toolkit. By the end you should have the languages we use (R and Python), the publishing system that turns code and prose into documents (Quarto, with a small LaTeX distribution for PDFs), and, most importantly, a comfortable place to write and run code: an editor or IDE.
We spend far more time in this chapter on the editor than on any single language. That is deliberate. Over the course of a graduate degree you will spend hundreds of hours writing scripts, documents, and analyses, and almost all of that time is spent inside an editor. Learning its layout, shortcuts, and quirks early is the single best productivity investment you can make.






NoteWhat each of these tools actually is



The install list below mixes three different kinds of software, and it helps to know which does what:

R, Python, and LaTeX are languages. You write code (or markup) in them and a program executes it: R and Python turn analysis code into results and figures; LaTeX turns markup into a typeset document and is what produces PDF output.
Quarto is a formatting and publishing system. It weaves your prose together with code chunks, runs the code through R or Python, and renders the result into an HTML page, slide deck, or PDF. It is the layer that turns a .qmd file into a finished document.
VS Code, Positron, and RStudio are integrated development environments (IDEs): the workbenches you sit in. Each gives you an editor, a place to run code and see output, and tools for managing projects. None of them is a language, and none is required by any other tool; they are where you do the work.

In short: R, Python, and LaTeX are languages, Quarto stitches and publishes them, and the IDEs are where you write.




Every program you write in this course, whether a Bash script, an R analysis, or a Quarto document, is a plain-text file. In principle you could write it with any tool that produces plain text, and for quick edits on a remote server, terminal editors such as nano and vim remain useful (we will meet them in ?@sec-unix-fundamentals). But plain editors do not scale to real projects. Once your work spans a dozen files across several directories, you want a tool that can show the whole project at once, that color-codes your code so structure and mistakes are visible at a glance, and that lets you run code right where you write it.
An Integrated Development Environment (IDE) bundles those capabilities into one window: a text editor with syntax highlighting and completion, a terminal for shell commands, a console for an interactive R or Python session, and tools such as a file explorer, a search across the project, and an interface to version control (?@sec-git-github). The three IDEs you will encounter in this course, VS Code, Positron, and RStudio, all provide these pieces; they differ mainly in emphasis, as we discuss in Section 1.7.






TipOpen the folder, not the file



All three IDEs work best when they can see your entire project. Always use File → Open Folder (or its equivalent) on the project’s top-level directory, rather than double-clicking a single file. The file explorer then shows the whole tree, project-wide search works, and the integrated terminal opens in that folder automatically, so relative paths in your scripts behave as expected.





Before installing anything, make sure your machine can handle the software. The course requires a laptop with 16 GB of RAM (8 GB is the absolute minimum and will struggle with larger datasets later in the term), at least 20 GB of free disk space (the installs in this chapter alone take roughly 10 GB, and your data needs room too), and an up-to-date macOS, Windows 10/11, or Linux. You also need administrator rights to install software; if your laptop is managed by a lab or department, you may need to ask their IT staff for help. Chromebooks and iPads will not work for this course. If you do not have a suitable laptop, talk to the instructor early so that a solution can be found.
Some installers, R in particular, come in different versions for different processors, so it helps to know what kind of chip you have. Table 1 shows how to find out.



Table 1: Finding out which processor your computer has










System
How to check
What you will see




macOS
Apple menu → About This Mac
Chip: Apple M1/M2/M3/M4 (Apple silicon) or Processor: Intel


Windows
Settings → System → About
Processor, RAM, “64-bit operating system”


Any Unix shell
uname -m
arm64 (Apple silicon or other ARM) or x86_64 (Intel/AMD)






While you are there, note your RAM and free disk space. In ?@sec-computing-at-uo we compare these numbers to what a single node of the Talapas cluster offers; the comparison is instructive.



Here is everything you need to install for the course, in a sensible order. Several of the downloads are large, so it is worth starting them and letting them run while you read the rest of the chapter. The operating-system prerequisites (the Xcode command-line tools on macOS, and WSL with Ubuntu on Windows) are covered in ?@sec-introduction; make sure those are finished first.


On macOS and Linux you already have one: open Terminal (on macOS, press Cmd-Space and type “Terminal”; on Linux, often Ctrl-Alt-T). On Windows, the shell you will use for this course is the Ubuntu app installed by WSL. Confirm it works by typing echo $SHELL and whoami at the prompt. macOS uses zsh by default and Ubuntu uses bash; for everything in this course they behave the same.



Download R from CRAN at https://cran.r-project.org. On macOS choose the .pkg installer that matches your chip: arm64 for Apple silicon (M1 through M4) or x86_64 for Intel Macs. If you are unsure, run uname -m in Terminal (Table 1). On Windows, choose “base” and run the installer, accepting the defaults. R is the subject of ?@sec-r-programming and everything that follows it.






NoteWindows: install R and Python on the Windows side



If you use WSL, install R, Python, VS Code, and Positron as ordinary Windows applications, not inside Ubuntu. The IDEs run on Windows and will find the Windows copies of R and Python; Ubuntu is where you will type shell commands. Section 1.8 explains how to tell the two apart.





There are three common ways to install Python 3, and for this course any of them is fine as long as you pick one and stick with it:

The python.org installer (simplest). Download from https://www.python.org/downloads/. On macOS, run the installer. On Windows, the first screen of the installer has a checkbox labeled “Add python.exe to PATH”: check it. If you skip it, your terminal will not be able to find Python and you will end up reinstalling.
uv (fastest). A single small program from https://docs.astral.sh/uv/ that installs Python versions, creates environments, and installs packages; uv python install 3.12 fetches an interpreter.
conda (Miniconda or Miniforge). A package manager that also installs non-Python software; it is the standard on Talapas and in bioinformatics, but heavier than the other two.

Inside Ubuntu on WSL, Python is already present, but the tools for installing packages and creating environments are not, so add them with:
sudo apt install -y python3-pip python3-venv
The trade-offs among these options, and how to use environments with each, are covered in ?@sec-python-programming.



Quarto turns Markdown and code into HTML pages, PDFs, Word documents, and slides; it is how this book and the course slides are built. Download the installer for your operating system from https://quarto.org/docs/get-started/ and run it. Quarto is covered in depth in ?@sec-quarto-documents.



To produce PDFs, Quarto needs a LaTeX distribution, the standard system for typesetting mathematics (?@sec-latex-basics). Full distributions such as MacTeX and MiKTeX are several gigabytes; TinyTeX installs only what Quarto needs. After Quarto is installed, open a terminal and run:
quarto --version
quarto install tinytex     # takes several minutes
If you already have a full LaTeX distribution, Quarto will find and use it, and you can skip this step.



Download Visual Studio Code from https://code.visualstudio.com/download. It is free and requires no account. Run the installer, open VS Code, and allow any permissions it asks for. Installation details and the extensions we use are in Section 1.4.



Download Positron from https://positron.posit.co/download. Install R and Python before Positron so that it can find them automatically. Details are in Section 1.5.



Several R and Python packages (and nearly all Bioconductor packages) compile from source the first time you install them, which requires a working C, C++, and often Fortran compiler. Install the toolchain once now; Section 1.13 lists the errors you will see if it is missing.
macOS. Apple’s Xcode command-line tools, installed in ?@sec-introduction with xcode-select --install, provide clang, git, and make. They do not include a Fortran compiler, which some R packages need; if you ever see gfortran not found, install gfortran from the R for macOS tools page at https://mac.r-project.org/tools/, then relaunch your IDE.
Windows. Install Rtools from https://cran.r-project.org/bin/windows/Rtools/, choosing the version that matches your R (for example Rtools44 for R 4.4, Rtools45 for R 4.5). Rtools is for the Windows copy of R; it is separate from Ubuntu on WSL, which uses build-essential as described next.
Linux (including Ubuntu on WSL). Install the toolchain from the package manager:
sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y build-essential gfortran
build-essential provides gcc, g++, and make; gfortran covers packages with Fortran code. On Fedora or RHEL, use sudo dnf groupinstall "Development Tools" and add gcc-gfortran.



We will also use Git for version control, but not yet. Installing and configuring Git, and connecting it to GitHub, is done in ?@sec-git-github, so there is nothing to do now.




VS Code is a free, general-purpose code editor from Microsoft, built on the open-source Code OSS project. It runs on macOS, Windows, and Linux, supports essentially every programming language through extensions, and has the largest extension ecosystem and user community of any editor. It is also the editor most likely to be waiting for you on a collaborator’s machine or in a company.


After running the installer from https://code.visualstudio.com/download, open VS Code and use File → Open Folder to open your project directory. Windows users will be prompted to install the WSL extension; accept, because it allows VS Code to work directly inside Ubuntu. Once the WSL extension is installed, typing code . in an Ubuntu terminal opens the current directory in VS Code, connected to Ubuntu.
On macOS, the code command is not on your PATH by default. Open the Command Palette (Cmd-Shift-P), type “shell command”, and run “Shell Command: Install ‘code’ command in PATH”. From then on, code . in Terminal opens the current folder, and code somefile.R opens a single file.



VS Code’s window has a handful of regions that you will use constantly. The Activity Bar runs down the far left and switches the side panel between the Explorer (a file tree of your open folder), Search (find text across the entire project), Source Control (a graphical front-end to Git, covered in ?@sec-git-github), and Extensions. The editor occupies the center; you can open many files in tabs and split the editor to see two files side by side with Cmd-\ (macOS) or Ctrl-\ (Windows/Linux). The integrated terminal at the bottom is a full shell (zsh, bash, or, on Windows with the WSL extension, Ubuntu’s bash); toggle it with Ctrl-`, the backtick key that sits above Tab. Finally, the Command Palette, opened with Cmd-Shift-P or Ctrl-Shift-P, lets you find and run any command by typing part of its name. If you cannot remember where a menu item lives, the Command Palette is the answer.



Open the Extensions panel (Cmd-Shift-X / Ctrl-Shift-X), search for each of the following, and click Install:

Quarto (from Quarto), to edit, preview, and render .qmd documents
Python (from Microsoft), for Python language support
R (from REditorSupport), for R language support
Jupyter (from Microsoft), for notebooks and interactive Python
WSL (from Microsoft; Windows only), to work inside Ubuntu
Later in the term, Remote - SSH (from Microsoft), which lets you edit files on Talapas as if they were local (?@sec-hpc-talapas)

Extensions can be added and removed at any time, so start with this short list and add more as you discover a need.



A few shortcuts account for most of the time savings in an editor. Table 2 lists the ones worth learning first; they work identically in Positron. A fuller list, including shell and RStudio shortcuts, is in ?@sec-appendix-shortcuts.



Table 2: Keyboard shortcuts in VS Code and Positron





Action

Positron is a free, next-generation data-science IDE from Posit, the company behind RStudio. It is built on Code OSS, the open-source core of VS Code, so everything in the previous section (Explorer, editor tabs, terminal, Command Palette, the shortcuts in Table 2) carries over unchanged. What Positron adds is a set of data-science panes of the kind RStudio users have relied on for years, and native support for both R and Python.


Download Positron from https://positron.posit.co/download and run the installer. Because Positron discovers the R and Python installations on your computer when it starts, install both languages first. Then open Positron, use File → Open Folder on your project, and start an R or Python session from the interpreter picker at the top right of the window. You can have several sessions open and switch among them, which is convenient for projects that mix R and Python.



In addition to the VS Code regions, Positron adds a Console, an interactive R or Python session where you can type expressions and see results immediately; a Variables pane listing every object you have created, with its type and size; a Plots pane that displays your figures and keeps a history of them; a Data Explorer that opens a data frame in a spreadsheet-like, sortable, filterable view; and a Help pane showing documentation for the function under your cursor. The recommended workflow is the same as in RStudio: write code in the editor, where it is saved in a file, and send lines or selections to the console with Cmd-Enter (macOS) or Ctrl-Enter (Windows/Linux). Use the console directly only for quick experiments; anything you would want to reproduce belongs in a file.



Positron installs extensions from Open VSX, an open extension registry, rather than from Microsoft’s Visual Studio Marketplace. Most extensions you would want (Quarto, Python, Jupyter, and many others) are available there, but a few Microsoft-only extensions are not, and Positron provides its own equivalents for the important ones. In particular, the VS Code R extension is not used in Positron: R support is built in, so do not install it.




RStudio, also from Posit, is the IDE that most R users learned on, and it remains an excellent environment for pure R work. Its window is divided into four panes: the Source editor for scripts and documents, the Console for a live R session, an Environment/History pane that shows your objects and past commands, and a Files/Plots/Packages/Help pane. If you already know and like RStudio, there is no need to abandon it; it renders Quarto documents, integrates with Git, and is available on Talapas through Open OnDemand (?@sec-computing-at-uo). It does not, however, support Python and other languages nearly as well as Positron or VS Code. RStudio is introduced in detail alongside R in ?@sec-rstudio.



Because Positron is built on Code OSS, VS Code and Positron share their editor, Command Palette, terminal, keyboard shortcuts, settings format, and Quarto support; both are free, cross-platform, support extensions, and can connect to remote machines over SSH. The difference is focus. Positron is built for data science: R and Python are first-class, and the Console, Variables, Plots, and Data Explorer panes are always at hand. VS Code is general-purpose: any language works through extensions, its extension library and community are the largest, and it is the tool of choice for shell scripts, configuration files, and polyglot projects. RStudio is R-centric and mature, with the best-integrated R experience but limited support for anything else. Table 3 summarizes the trade-offs, and Table 4 gives a rule of thumb.

You do not have to choose forever. VS Code and Positron share so much muscle memory that learning one means you mostly know the other, and this course uses both.



With WSL installed, a Windows laptop effectively runs two operating systems: Windows itself and Ubuntu. Both are useful, but it matters which one you are typing into, because they have different home directories, different views of the file system, and different commands. Table 5 is the map.

The rule for this course is simple: type shell commands in Ubuntu, and install R, Python, VS Code, and Positron on the Windows side. In VS Code, a green badge in the bottom-left corner reading WSL: Ubuntu tells you that the window is connected to Ubuntu; without it, the integrated terminal is PowerShell and Unix commands will mostly fail. Your Linux home directory (/home/you) lives on a virtual disk and is the fastest place to work; your Windows files are reachable from Ubuntu under /mnt/c/ (for example /mnt/c/Users/you/Documents), and Ubuntu’s files appear in Windows File Explorer under Linux in the sidebar, or at the path \\wsl$\Ubuntu\home\you. Installing Windows Terminal from the Microsoft Store gives you a nicer terminal with tabs that can open either side.






TipKeep projects in the Linux home directory



WSL and Windows share files, so you never need two copies of anything, but where a project lives affects speed. Working inside the Linux home directory (~, that is /home/you) is noticeably faster than working under /mnt/c, and case-sensitivity rules differ between the two file systems. Keep course projects in your Linux home and reach over to /mnt/c/Users/you/Downloads only when you need a file that arrived on the Windows side. If you later run R or Python inside Ubuntu, keep the project under ~/ as well; running a WSL program on files under /mnt/c is the most common cause of mysteriously slow file reading.





Two file formats let you mix code, its output, and explanatory text in one document, and you will encounter both. A Jupyter notebook (.ipynb) is made of cells, each containing code or Markdown, and the outputs are saved inside the file alongside the code. Notebooks are enormously popular in Python, machine learning, and image analysis; they run in JupyterLab, VS Code, and Positron, and on Talapas through Open OnDemand (?@sec-computing-at-uo). Their drawback is that the file is stored as JSON with embedded output, which makes it hard to read as text and awkward to track in Git.
A Quarto document (.qmd) is plain text: Markdown prose with a YAML header and code chunks in R, Python, Julia, or Bash. Output is not stored in the source; it is regenerated every time you render, which is exactly what reproducibility demands, and the plain-text source is easy to read, edit, and diff in Git. Quarto renders to HTML, PDF, Word, slides, and websites (?@sec-quarto-documents). You do not have to choose between the two: Quarto can render Jupyter notebooks directly with quarto render notebook.ipynb, and can use Jupyter as the engine for Python chunks in .qmd files. This course uses Quarto; many of your labs may use Jupyter, and the skills transfer.



Different projects need different versions of packages, and installing everything into one Python installation eventually breaks something. The solution is an environment: an isolated set of packages for one project. Python’s built-in venv module creates one in your project folder:
python3 -m venv .venv            # create an environment in this project
source .venv/bin/activate        # turn it on (Windows PowerShell: .venv\Scripts\activate)
pip install numpy pandas         # install packages into it
deactivate                       # turn it off
While the environment is active, python and pip refer to the copies inside .venv, and packages you install go there rather than into the system Python. On Talapas you will instead use conda environments, which can manage non-Python software as well (?@sec-hpc-talapas); uv is a fast, modern alternative to venv and pip; and R has the same idea in the renv package. There is nothing to set up now; the point is to know the word “environment” so that it is not a surprise later.



Both IDEs can host an AI coding assistant. GitHub Copilot in VS Code suggests code as you type and answers questions in a chat panel; it is free for verified students through the GitHub Student Developer Pack. Positron Assistant is an AI chat built into Positron that can see your console, variables, and plots. Both are genuinely useful for explaining error messages, writing boilerplate, and learning unfamiliar syntax.
They are also confidently wrong surprisingly often. Treat every suggestion as a draft from a well-read but careless colleague: read it, run it, and make sure you understand it before it goes into your analysis. Never paste sensitive data (see the data-classification rules in ?@sec-computing-at-uo) into an assistant, and follow the course’s AI policy: you may use these tools to learn and debug, but the work you submit must be your own. We return to AI-assisted coding, and how to use it well, in ?@sec-ai-assisted-coding; there is no need to set anything up now.



Once everything is installed, open a terminal inside VS Code or Positron (Ctrl-`) and run the following commands:
echo $SHELL
R --version
python3 --version     # Windows PowerShell (not WSL): try  py --version
quarto --version
quarto check          # checks for R, Python, and LaTeX
Each should print a version number (or, for quarto check, a list of passing checks), not “command not found.” Then open Positron and confirm that you can start both an R console and a Python console from the interpreter picker. If a command is not found, the most likely explanation is that the terminal was opened before the program was installed: a terminal only sees programs that were on the PATH when it started, so close and reopen the terminal, or restart the IDE, before doing anything else. Table 6 lists other common problems.

If you are still stuck, copy the exact error message as text and ask for help; ?@sec-computing-at-uo describes where to ask at UO and how to ask so that you get a fast answer.



Table 6 covers the problems that appear while installing. The following come up a little later, usually the first time you install R packages or start a real project, and every one of them has bitten several students in past years.


The Xcode command-line tools are missing or out of date. In Terminal:
xcode-select --install
Relaunch RStudio or Positron after the install finishes. If the error instead mentions gfortran not found or library not found for -lgfortran, install gfortran from https://mac.r-project.org/tools/ (see the compiler tools item in Section 1.3) and try the package install again.



R is trying to compile a package but cannot find Rtools, or you have an Rtools version that does not match your R version (Rtools44 for R 4.4, and so on). Install the matching version from https://cran.r-project.org/bin/windows/Rtools/, restart R, and confirm with Sys.which("make"), which should now print a path.



The most common cause is a slow Bioconductor mirror. Pick a closer one and try again:
chooseBioCmirror()                              # interactive; pick a US mirror
options(BioC_mirror = "https://bioconductor.org")
BiocManager::install("DESeq2")
The first Bioconductor install compiles many dependencies and can genuinely take 20 to 60 minutes; do it the day before you need it, not the morning of.



Almost always a stale R session: the package was installed, but the running session was started before. Restart R (Session → Restart R, or Ctrl/Cmd + Shift + F10) and try library() again. If that does not help, the package may have been installed into the library of a different R version than the one the IDE is running:
.libPaths()                          # which library folders is this session using?
installed.packages()[, "Package"]    # what is actually installed there?
R.version.string                     # which R is this?
If the versions do not match, point the IDE at the correct R install (RStudio: Tools → Global Options → General → R version; Positron: the interpreter picker at the top right) and reinstall the package there.



The project is on the Windows side (/mnt/c/Users/...) but the program is running inside WSL, or the reverse. File access across that boundary is dramatically slower, and case-sensitivity differs. Choose one arrangement and stick with it: either run R, Python, and the IDE as Windows programs with the project under C:\Users\you, which is what this course recommends (Section 1.8), or run everything inside Ubuntu with the project under ~/.



R keeps every object you create for the whole session, so a later chunk can silently use an old object after you edit an earlier one. Restart R and run the script from the top; rm(list = ls()) clears variables but not loaded packages, so a restart is more reliable. In RStudio, also go to Tools → Global Options → General and uncheck “Restore .RData into workspace at startup” and set “Save workspace to .RData on exit” to Never, so that each session starts clean.




This chapter assembled the software you will use for the rest of the course and, more importantly, introduced the place where you will do most of your work: the editor. Key takeaways:

An IDE combines an editor, terminal, console, and project tools in one window; always open the whole project folder, not a single file
The core installs are R (matching your chip), Python (with “Add to PATH” on Windows), Quarto with TinyTeX, VS Code, and Positron; Git comes later in ?@sec-git-github
VS Code is general-purpose with the largest ecosystem; Positron is built on the same core with R and Python and data-science panes built in; RStudio remains a fine choice for pure R
On Windows, type shell commands in Ubuntu but install languages and IDEs on the Windows side, and watch for the “WSL: Ubuntu” badge
Quarto documents are plain text and regenerate their output; Jupyter notebooks store output in the file; Quarto can render both
Python environments (venv, conda, uv) and R’s renv isolate each project’s packages
Editor-based AI assistants are useful for learning and debugging but must be read, tested, and never fed sensitive data
Compiling packages needs a toolchain: Xcode command-line tools plus gfortran on macOS, Rtools matching your R version on Windows, build-essential gfortran on Linux
R --version, python3 --version, quarto --version, and quarto check confirm a working installation; when a command is not found, reopen the terminal first
The most common later problems (compiler errors, slow Bioconductor mirrors, a stale R session, projects on the wrong side of WSL) are collected in Section 1.13

In ?@sec-computing-at-uo we turn from your laptop to the resources the University provides: your digital identity, cloud storage, data-security rules, site-licensed software, and the Talapas cluster.









TipPractice Exercises




Checkpoint: Run every command in Section 1.12 and record the version of R, Python, and Quarto on your machine. Note which shell echo $SHELL reports and whether quarto check finds LaTeX.
Project layout: Create a folder called bootcamp with subfolders data/raw, data/processed, scripts, output/figures, and docs. Open the folder in VS Code and in Positron. In each, open the integrated terminal and run pwd to confirm it started in your project directory.
Extensions: Install the Quarto, Python, R, and Jupyter extensions in VS Code (and, on Windows, WSL). Then open Positron’s Extensions panel and confirm that the Quarto extension is available from Open VSX. What happens if you search for the R extension there?
Shortcuts: In a new file, type three lines of code, select them, and use the toggle-comment shortcut from Table 2 to comment and uncomment them. Then use the project-wide search to find every occurrence of the word library in your bootcamp folder.
Windows only: Open a PowerShell window and an Ubuntu window side by side. In each, print your home directory (echo $HOME in Ubuntu; echo $HOME or $env:USERPROFILE in PowerShell) and list its contents. Then, from Ubuntu, ls /mnt/c/Users/<your name> and confirm you can see your Windows files.

title: Your Computational Toolkit: Installing and Using Editors and IDEs
text:
Every program you write in this course, whether a Bash script, an R analysis, or a Quarto document, is a plain-text file. In principle you could write it with any tool that produces plain text, and for quick edits on a remote server, terminal editors such as nano and vim remain useful (we will meet them in ?@sec-unix-fundamentals). But plain editors do not scale to real projects. Once your work spans a dozen files across several directories, you want a tool that can show the whole project at once, that color-codes your code so structure and mistakes are visible at a glance, and that lets you run code right where you write it.
An Integrated Development Environment (IDE) bundles those capabilities into one window: a text editor with syntax highlighting and completion, a terminal for shell commands, a console for an interactive R or Python session, and tools such as a file explorer, a search across the project, and an interface to version control (?@sec-git-github). The three IDEs you will encounter in this course, VS Code, Positron, and RStudio, all provide these pieces; they differ mainly in emphasis, as we discuss in Section 1.7.






TipOpen the folder, not the file



All three IDEs work best when they can see your entire project. Always use File → Open Folder (or its equivalent) on the project’s top-level directory, rather than double-clicking a single file. The file explorer then shows the whole tree, project-wide search works, and the integrated terminal opens in that folder automatically, so relative paths in your scripts behave as expected.

title: Your Computational Toolkit: Installing and Using Editors and IDEs
text:
Before installing anything, make sure your machine can handle the software. The course requires a laptop with 16 GB of RAM (8 GB is the absolute minimum and will struggle with larger datasets later in the term), at least 20 GB of free disk space (the installs in this chapter alone take roughly 10 GB, and your data needs room too), and an up-to-date macOS, Windows 10/11, or Linux. You also need administrator rights to install software; if your laptop is managed by a lab or department, you may need to ask their IT staff for help. Chromebooks and iPads will not work for this course. If you do not have a suitable laptop, talk to the instructor early so that a solution can be found.
Some installers, R in particular, come in different versions for different processors, so it helps to know what kind of chip you have. Table 1 shows how to find out.



Table 1: Finding out which processor your computer has










System
How to check
What you will see




macOS
Apple menu → About This Mac
Chip: Apple M1/M2/M3/M4 (Apple silicon) or Processor: Intel


Windows
Settings → System → About
Processor, RAM, “64-bit operating system”


Any Unix shell
uname -m
arm64 (Apple silicon or other ARM) or x86_64 (Intel/AMD)






While you are there, note your RAM and free disk space. In ?@sec-computing-at-uo we compare these numbers to what a single node of the Talapas cluster offers; the comparison is instructive.

title: Your Computational Toolkit: Installing and Using Editors and IDEs
text:
Here is everything you need to install for the course, in a sensible order. Several of the downloads are large, so it is worth starting them and letting them run while you read the rest of the chapter. The operating-system prerequisites (the Xcode command-line tools on macOS, and WSL with Ubuntu on Windows) are covered in ?@sec-introduction; make sure those are finished first.


On macOS and Linux you already have one: open Terminal (on macOS, press Cmd-Space and type “Terminal”; on Linux, often Ctrl-Alt-T). On Windows, the shell you will use for this course is the Ubuntu app installed by WSL. Confirm it works by typing echo $SHELL and whoami at the prompt. macOS uses zsh by default and Ubuntu uses bash; for everything in this course they behave the same.



Download R from CRAN at https://cran.r-project.org. On macOS choose the .pkg installer that matches your chip: arm64 for Apple silicon (M1 through M4) or x86_64 for Intel Macs. If you are unsure, run uname -m in Terminal (Table 1). On Windows, choose “base” and run the installer, accepting the defaults. R is the subject of ?@sec-r-programming and everything that follows it.






NoteWindows: install R and Python on the Windows side



If you use WSL, install R, Python, VS Code, and Positron as ordinary Windows applications, not inside Ubuntu. The IDEs run on Windows and will find the Windows copies of R and Python; Ubuntu is where you will type shell commands. Section 1.8 explains how to tell the two apart.





There are three common ways to install Python 3, and for this course any of them is fine as long as you pick one and stick with it:

The python.org installer (simplest). Download from https://www.python.org/downloads/. On macOS, run the installer. On Windows, the first screen of the installer has a checkbox labeled “Add python.exe to PATH”: check it. If you skip it, your terminal will not be able to find Python and you will end up reinstalling.
uv (fastest). A single small program from https://docs.astral.sh/uv/ that installs Python versions, creates environments, and installs packages; uv python install 3.12 fetches an interpreter.
conda (Miniconda or Miniforge). A package manager that also installs non-Python software; it is the standard on Talapas and in bioinformatics, but heavier than the other two.

Inside Ubuntu on WSL, Python is already present, but the tools for installing packages and creating environments are not, so add them with:
sudo apt install -y python3-pip python3-venv
The trade-offs among these options, and how to use environments with each, are covered in ?@sec-python-programming.



Quarto turns Markdown and code into HTML pages, PDFs, Word documents, and slides; it is how this book and the course slides are built. Download the installer for your operating system from https://quarto.org/docs/get-started/ and run it. Quarto is covered in depth in ?@sec-quarto-documents.



To produce PDFs, Quarto needs a LaTeX distribution, the standard system for typesetting mathematics (?@sec-latex-basics). Full distributions such as MacTeX and MiKTeX are several gigabytes; TinyTeX installs only what Quarto needs. After Quarto is installed, open a terminal and run:
quarto --version
quarto install tinytex     # takes several minutes
If you already have a full LaTeX distribution, Quarto will find and use it, and you can skip this step.



Download Visual Studio Code from https://code.visualstudio.com/download. It is free and requires no account. Run the installer, open VS Code, and allow any permissions it asks for. Installation details and the extensions we use are in Section 1.4.



Download Positron from https://positron.posit.co/download. Install R and Python before Positron so that it can find them automatically. Details are in Section 1.5.



Several R and Python packages (and nearly all Bioconductor packages) compile from source the first time you install them, which requires a working C, C++, and often Fortran compiler. Install the toolchain once now; Section 1.13 lists the errors you will see if it is missing.
macOS. Apple’s Xcode command-line tools, installed in ?@sec-introduction with xcode-select --install, provide clang, git, and make. They do not include a Fortran compiler, which some R packages need; if you ever see gfortran not found, install gfortran from the R for macOS tools page at https://mac.r-project.org/tools/, then relaunch your IDE.
Windows. Install Rtools from https://cran.r-project.org/bin/windows/Rtools/, choosing the version that matches your R (for example Rtools44 for R 4.4, Rtools45 for R 4.5). Rtools is for the Windows copy of R; it is separate from Ubuntu on WSL, which uses build-essential as described next.
Linux (including Ubuntu on WSL). Install the toolchain from the package manager:
sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y build-essential gfortran
build-essential provides gcc, g++, and make; gfortran covers packages with Fortran code. On Fedora or RHEL, use sudo dnf groupinstall "Development Tools" and add gcc-gfortran.



We will also use Git for version control, but not yet. Installing and configuring Git, and connecting it to GitHub, is done in ?@sec-git-github, so there is nothing to do now.

title: Your Computational Toolkit: Installing and Using Editors and IDEs
text:
VS Code is a free, general-purpose code editor from Microsoft, built on the open-source Code OSS project. It runs on macOS, Windows, and Linux, supports essentially every programming language through extensions, and has the largest extension ecosystem and user community of any editor. It is also the editor most likely to be waiting for you on a collaborator’s machine or in a company.


After running the installer from https://code.visualstudio.com/download, open VS Code and use File → Open Folder to open your project directory. Windows users will be prompted to install the WSL extension; accept, because it allows VS Code to work directly inside Ubuntu. Once the WSL extension is installed, typing code . in an Ubuntu terminal opens the current directory in VS Code, connected to Ubuntu.
On macOS, the code command is not on your PATH by default. Open the Command Palette (Cmd-Shift-P), type “shell command”, and run “Shell Command: Install ‘code’ command in PATH”. From then on, code . in Terminal opens the current folder, and code somefile.R opens a single file.



VS Code’s window has a handful of regions that you will use constantly. The Activity Bar runs down the far left and switches the side panel between the Explorer (a file tree of your open folder), Search (find text across the entire project), Source Control (a graphical front-end to Git, covered in ?@sec-git-github), and Extensions. The editor occupies the center; you can open many files in tabs and split the editor to see two files side by side with Cmd-\ (macOS) or Ctrl-\ (Windows/Linux). The integrated terminal at the bottom is a full shell (zsh, bash, or, on Windows with the WSL extension, Ubuntu’s bash); toggle it with Ctrl-`, the backtick key that sits above Tab. Finally, the Command Palette, opened with Cmd-Shift-P or Ctrl-Shift-P, lets you find and run any command by typing part of its name. If you cannot remember where a menu item lives, the Command Palette is the answer.



Open the Extensions panel (Cmd-Shift-X / Ctrl-Shift-X), search for each of the following, and click Install:

Quarto (from Quarto), to edit, preview, and render .qmd documents
Python (from Microsoft), for Python language support
R (from REditorSupport), for R language support
Jupyter (from Microsoft), for notebooks and interactive Python
WSL (from Microsoft; Windows only), to work inside Ubuntu
Later in the term, Remote - SSH (from Microsoft), which lets you edit files on Talapas as if they were local (?@sec-hpc-talapas)

Extensions can be added and removed at any time, so start with this short list and add more as you discover a need.



A few shortcuts account for most of the time savings in an editor. Table 2 lists the ones worth learning first; they work identically in Positron. A fuller list, including shell and RStudio shortcuts, is in ?@sec-appendix-shortcuts.

title: Your Computational Toolkit: Installing and Using Editors and IDEs
text:
Positron is a free, next-generation data-science IDE from Posit, the company behind RStudio. It is built on Code OSS, the open-source core of VS Code, so everything in the previous section (Explorer, editor tabs, terminal, Command Palette, the shortcuts in Table 2) carries over unchanged. What Positron adds is a set of data-science panes of the kind RStudio users have relied on for years, and native support for both R and Python.


Download Positron from https://positron.posit.co/download and run the installer. Because Positron discovers the R and Python installations on your computer when it starts, install both languages first. Then open Positron, use File → Open Folder on your project, and start an R or Python session from the interpreter picker at the top right of the window. You can have several sessions open and switch among them, which is convenient for projects that mix R and Python.



In addition to the VS Code regions, Positron adds a Console, an interactive R or Python session where you can type expressions and see results immediately; a Variables pane listing every object you have created, with its type and size; a Plots pane that displays your figures and keeps a history of them; a Data Explorer that opens a data frame in a spreadsheet-like, sortable, filterable view; and a Help pane showing documentation for the function under your cursor. The recommended workflow is the same as in RStudio: write code in the editor, where it is saved in a file, and send lines or selections to the console with Cmd-Enter (macOS) or Ctrl-Enter (Windows/Linux). Use the console directly only for quick experiments; anything you would want to reproduce belongs in a file.



Positron installs extensions from Open VSX, an open extension registry, rather than from Microsoft’s Visual Studio Marketplace. Most extensions you would want (Quarto, Python, Jupyter, and many others) are available there, but a few Microsoft-only extensions are not, and Positron provides its own equivalents for the important ones. In particular, the VS Code R extension is not used in Positron: R support is built in, so do not install it.

title: Your Computational Toolkit: Installing and Using Editors and IDEs
text: RStudio, also from Posit, is the IDE that most R users learned on, and it remains an excellent environment for pure R work. Its window is divided into four panes: the Source editor for scripts and documents, the Console for a live R session, an Environment/History pane that shows your objects and past commands, and a Files/Plots/Packages/Help pane. If you already know and like RStudio, there is no need to abandon it; it renders Quarto documents, integrates with Git, and is available on Talapas through Open OnDemand (?@sec-computing-at-uo). It does not, however, support Python and other languages nearly as well as Positron or VS Code. RStudio is introduced in detail alongside R in ?@sec-rstudio.

title: Your Computational Toolkit: Installing and Using Editors and IDEs
text:
Because Positron is built on Code OSS, VS Code and Positron share their editor, Command Palette, terminal, keyboard shortcuts, settings format, and Quarto support; both are free, cross-platform, support extensions, and can connect to remote machines over SSH. The difference is focus. Positron is built for data science: R and Python are first-class, and the Console, Variables, Plots, and Data Explorer panes are always at hand. VS Code is general-purpose: any language works through extensions, its extension library and community are the largest, and it is the tool of choice for shell scripts, configuration files, and polyglot projects. RStudio is R-centric and mature, with the best-integrated R experience but limited support for anything else. Table 3 summarizes the trade-offs, and Table 4 gives a rule of thumb.

title: Your Computational Toolkit: Installing and Using Editors and IDEs
text:
With WSL installed, a Windows laptop effectively runs two operating systems: Windows itself and Ubuntu. Both are useful, but it matters which one you are typing into, because they have different home directories, different views of the file system, and different commands. Table 5 is the map.



Table 5: Windows and Ubuntu on the same laptop











Windows side
Ubuntu (WSL) side




Terminal
PowerShell or Command Prompt
The Ubuntu app, or a VS Code terminal showing “WSL: Ubuntu”


Prompt looks like
PS C:\Users\you>
you@laptop:~$


Your home folder
C:\Users\you
/home/you (also ~)


The other side’s files
\\wsl$\Ubuntu\home\you
/mnt/c/Users/you


Unix commands (ls, grep, …)
Mostly no
Yes


Where R, Python, VS Code, Positron are installed
Here
(not needed)






The rule for this course is simple: type shell commands in Ubuntu, and install R, Python, VS Code, and Positron on the Windows side. In VS Code, a green badge in the bottom-left corner reading WSL: Ubuntu tells you that the window is connected to Ubuntu; without it, the integrated terminal is PowerShell and Unix commands will mostly fail. Your Linux home directory (/home/you) lives on a virtual disk and is the fastest place to work; your Windows files are reachable from Ubuntu under /mnt/c/ (for example /mnt/c/Users/you/Documents), and Ubuntu’s files appear in Windows File Explorer under Linux in the sidebar, or at the path \\wsl$\Ubuntu\home\you. Installing Windows Terminal from the Microsoft Store gives you a nicer terminal with tabs that can open either side.






TipKeep projects in the Linux home directory



WSL and Windows share files, so you never need two copies of anything, but where a project lives affects speed. Working inside the Linux home directory (~, that is /home/you) is noticeably faster than working under /mnt/c, and case-sensitivity rules differ between the two file systems. Keep course projects in your Linux home and reach over to /mnt/c/Users/you/Downloads only when you need a file that arrived on the Windows side. If you later run R or Python inside Ubuntu, keep the project under ~/ as well; running a WSL program on files under /mnt/c is the most common cause of mysteriously slow file reading.

title: Your Computational Toolkit: Installing and Using Editors and IDEs
text:
Two file formats let you mix code, its output, and explanatory text in one document, and you will encounter both. A Jupyter notebook (.ipynb) is made of cells, each containing code or Markdown, and the outputs are saved inside the file alongside the code. Notebooks are enormously popular in Python, machine learning, and image analysis; they run in JupyterLab, VS Code, and Positron, and on Talapas through Open OnDemand (?@sec-computing-at-uo). Their drawback is that the file is stored as JSON with embedded output, which makes it hard to read as text and awkward to track in Git.
A Quarto document (.qmd) is plain text: Markdown prose with a YAML header and code chunks in R, Python, Julia, or Bash. Output is not stored in the source; it is regenerated every time you render, which is exactly what reproducibility demands, and the plain-text source is easy to read, edit, and diff in Git. Quarto renders to HTML, PDF, Word, slides, and websites (?@sec-quarto-documents). You do not have to choose between the two: Quarto can render Jupyter notebooks directly with quarto render notebook.ipynb, and can use Jupyter as the engine for Python chunks in .qmd files. This course uses Quarto; many of your labs may use Jupyter, and the skills transfer.

title: Your Computational Toolkit: Installing and Using Editors and IDEs
text:
Different projects need different versions of packages, and installing everything into one Python installation eventually breaks something. The solution is an environment: an isolated set of packages for one project. Python’s built-in venv module creates one in your project folder:
python3 -m venv .venv            # create an environment in this project
source .venv/bin/activate        # turn it on (Windows PowerShell: .venv\Scripts\activate)
pip install numpy pandas         # install packages into it
deactivate                       # turn it off
While the environment is active, python and pip refer to the copies inside .venv, and packages you install go there rather than into the system Python. On Talapas you will instead use conda environments, which can manage non-Python software as well (?@sec-hpc-talapas); uv is a fast, modern alternative to venv and pip; and R has the same idea in the renv package. There is nothing to set up now; the point is to know the word “environment” so that it is not a surprise later.

title: Your Computational Toolkit: Installing and Using Editors and IDEs
text:
Both IDEs can host an AI coding assistant. GitHub Copilot in VS Code suggests code as you type and answers questions in a chat panel; it is free for verified students through the GitHub Student Developer Pack. Positron Assistant is an AI chat built into Positron that can see your console, variables, and plots. Both are genuinely useful for explaining error messages, writing boilerplate, and learning unfamiliar syntax.
They are also confidently wrong surprisingly often. Treat every suggestion as a draft from a well-read but careless colleague: read it, run it, and make sure you understand it before it goes into your analysis. Never paste sensitive data (see the data-classification rules in ?@sec-computing-at-uo) into an assistant, and follow the course’s AI policy: you may use these tools to learn and debug, but the work you submit must be your own. We return to AI-assisted coding, and how to use it well, in ?@sec-ai-assisted-coding; there is no need to set anything up now.

title: Your Computational Toolkit: Installing and Using Editors and IDEs
text:
Once everything is installed, open a terminal inside VS Code or Positron (Ctrl-`) and run the following commands:
echo $SHELL
R --version
python3 --version     # Windows PowerShell (not WSL): try  py --version
quarto --version
quarto check          # checks for R, Python, and LaTeX
Each should print a version number (or, for quarto check, a list of passing checks), not “command not found.” Then open Positron and confirm that you can start both an R console and a Python console from the interpreter picker. If a command is not found, the most likely explanation is that the terminal was opened before the program was installed: a terminal only sees programs that were on the PATH when it started, so close and reopen the terminal, or restart the IDE, before doing anything else. Table 6 lists other common problems.



Table 6: Troubleshooting common installation problems










Symptom
Likely cause
Try this

Close and reopen the terminal (or restart VS Code/Positron)


Windows: python opens the Microsoft Store
The Windows “app execution alias” intercepts the command
Use py instead, or reinstall Python with Add python.exe to PATH checked

Need administrator rights, or the file is not executable
Run the installer as administrator; on Unix, use sudo only when instructions say to


Installer fails or reports “disk full”

Right-click the app and choose Open, or allow it under System Settings → Privacy & Security

If you are still stuck, copy the exact error message as text and ask for help; ?@sec-computing-at-uo describes where to ask at UO and how to ask so that you get a fast answer.

title: Your Computational Toolkit: Installing and Using Editors and IDEs
text:
Table 6 covers the problems that appear while installing. The following come up a little later, usually the first time you install R packages or start a real project, and every one of them has bitten several students in past years.


The Xcode command-line tools are missing or out of date. In Terminal:
xcode-select --install
Relaunch RStudio or Positron after the install finishes. If the error instead mentions gfortran not found or library not found for -lgfortran, install gfortran from https://mac.r-project.org/tools/ (see the compiler tools item in Section 1.3) and try the package install again.



R is trying to compile a package but cannot find Rtools, or you have an Rtools version that does not match your R version (Rtools44 for R 4.4, and so on). Install the matching version from https://cran.r-project.org/bin/windows/Rtools/, restart R, and confirm with Sys.which("make"), which should now print a path.



The most common cause is a slow Bioconductor mirror. Pick a closer one and try again:
chooseBioCmirror()                              # interactive; pick a US mirror
options(BioC_mirror = "https://bioconductor.org")
BiocManager::install("DESeq2")
The first Bioconductor install compiles many dependencies and can genuinely take 20 to 60 minutes; do it the day before you need it, not the morning of.



Almost always a stale R session: the package was installed, but the running session was started before. Restart R (Session → Restart R, or Ctrl/Cmd + Shift + F10) and try library() again. If that does not help, the package may have been installed into the library of a different R version than the one the IDE is running:
.libPaths()                          # which library folders is this session using?
installed.packages()[, "Package"]    # what is actually installed there?
R.version.string                     # which R is this?
If the versions do not match, point the IDE at the correct R install (RStudio: Tools → Global Options → General → R version; Positron: the interpreter picker at the top right) and reinstall the package there.



The project is on the Windows side (/mnt/c/Users/...) but the program is running inside WSL, or the reverse. File access across that boundary is dramatically slower, and case-sensitivity differs. Choose one arrangement and stick with it: either run R, Python, and the IDE as Windows programs with the project under C:\Users\you, which is what this course recommends (Section 1.8), or run everything inside Ubuntu with the project under ~/.



R keeps every object you create for the whole session, so a later chunk can silently use an old object after you edit an earlier one. Restart R and run the script from the top; rm(list = ls()) clears variables but not loaded packages, so a restart is more reliable. In RStudio, also go to Tools → Global Options → General and uncheck “Restore .RData into workspace at startup” and set “Save workspace to .RData on exit” to Never, so that each session starts clean.

title: Your Computational Toolkit: Installing and Using Editors and IDEs
text:
This chapter assembled the software you will use for the rest of the course and, more importantly, introduced the place where you will do most of your work: the editor. Key takeaways:

An IDE combines an editor, terminal, console, and project tools in one window; always open the whole project folder, not a single file
The core installs are R (matching your chip), Python (with “Add to PATH” on Windows), Quarto with TinyTeX, VS Code, and Positron; Git comes later in ?@sec-git-github
VS Code is general-purpose with the largest ecosystem; Positron is built on the same core with R and Python and data-science panes built in; RStudio remains a fine choice for pure R
On Windows, type shell commands in Ubuntu but install languages and IDEs on the Windows side, and watch for the “WSL: Ubuntu” badge
Quarto documents are plain text and regenerate their output; Jupyter notebooks store output in the file; Quarto can render both
Python environments (venv, conda, uv) and R’s renv isolate each project’s packages
Editor-based AI assistants are useful for learning and debugging but must be read, tested, and never fed sensitive data
Compiling packages needs a toolchain: Xcode command-line tools plus gfortran on macOS, Rtools matching your R version on Windows, build-essential gfortran on Linux
R --version, python3 --version, quarto --version, and quarto check confirm a working installation; when a command is not found, reopen the terminal first
The most common later problems (compiler errors, slow Bioconductor mirrors, a stale R session, projects on the wrong side of WSL) are collected in Section 1.13

In ?@sec-computing-at-uo we turn from your laptop to the resources the University provides: your digital identity, cloud storage, data-security rules, site-licensed software, and the Talapas cluster.

title: Your Computational Toolkit: Installing and Using Editors and IDEs
text:
TipPractice Exercises




Checkpoint: Run every command in Section 1.12 and record the version of R, Python, and Quarto on your machine. Note which shell echo $SHELL reports and whether quarto check finds LaTeX.
Project layout: Create a folder called bootcamp with subfolders data/raw, data/processed, scripts, output/figures, and docs. Open the folder in VS Code and in Positron. In each, open the integrated terminal and run pwd to confirm it started in your project directory.
Extensions: Install the Quarto, Python, R, and Jupyter extensions in VS Code (and, on Windows, WSL). Then open Positron’s Extensions panel and confirm that the Quarto extension is available from Open VSX. What happens if you search for the R extension there?
Shortcuts: In a new file, type three lines of code, select them, and use the toggle-comment shortcut from Table 2 to comment and uncomment them. Then use the project-wide search to find every occurrence of the word library in your bootcamp folder.
Windows only: Open a PowerShell window and an Ubuntu window side by side. In each, print your home directory (echo $HOME in Ubuntu; echo $HOME or $env:USERPROFILE in PowerShell) and list its contents. Then, from Ubuntu, ls /mnt/c/Users/<your name> and confirm you can see your Windows files.

    | samtools sort -@ "$SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK" -o "$OUT.tmp"

#SBATCH --array=3,7,12          # Rerun only specific tasks

title: High-Performance Computing with Talapas
text:
NoteLearning Objectives



After completing this chapter, you will be able to:

Explain what high-performance computing (HPC) is and when to use it
Connect to Talapas via SSH, your editor’s Remote-SSH extension, and Open OnDemand
Navigate the storage system and understand quotas
Explain how the SLURM scheduler decides which job runs next (fair-share, backfill, QOS limits)
Write and submit batch jobs using SLURM
Monitor job status, interpret pending reasons, and right-size requests with seff and sacct
Use software modules, per-user environments, and containers
Design a multi-step, multi-sample pipeline that checkpoints, logs, and scales out with job arrays or a workflow manager
Follow best practices for responsible cluster use





When your laptop isn’t enough—when analyses run for days, require hundreds of gigabytes of memory, or need specialized hardware like GPUs—you need high-performance computing (HPC).
An HPC cluster is a collection of interconnected computers (called nodes) that work together to solve computational problems. Instead of upgrading your personal computer indefinitely, you submit jobs to a shared resource with far more capability.


Consider HPC when:

Analyses take hours or days on your laptop
Data is too large to fit in your computer’s memory
You need GPUs for machine learning
You want to run many similar jobs in parallel
Your analysis would monopolize your personal computer




Talapas is the University of Oregon’s HPC cluster, named after a Chinook word for coyote (the educator and keeper of knowledge). It’s managed by Research Advanced Computing Services (RACS).
Key resources:

Over 14,520 CPU cores
129 TB of total memory
89 GPUs (including NVIDIA A100 and H100)
3+ petabytes of storage





Understanding the cluster architecture (Figure 1; compare the generic layout in ?@fig-cluster-architecture) helps you use it effectively.

    U[Your Computer] --> SSH([SSH])
    SSH --> L1[Login Node 1]
    SSH --> L2[Login Node 2]

    L1 --> S[SLURM Scheduler]
    L2 --> S
    L3 --> S
    L4 --> S
    S --> C1[CPU Nodes]
    S --> C2[GPU Nodes]
    S --> C3[High-Memory Nodes]
    C1 --> ST[(Shared Storage)]
    C2 --> ST
    C3 --> ST

Figure 1: Talapas cluster architecture showing login nodes, scheduler, and compute nodes













WarningNever Run Jobs on Login Nodes



Login nodes are where you:

Log in and manage files
Edit scripts
Submit jobs
Check job status

Do NOT run computationally intensive work on login nodes! They’re shared by everyone, and heavy processes will be terminated.
Compute nodes are where your actual work runs, accessed through the job scheduler (SLURM) [@yoo2003slurm].

Across the whole cluster (general-use and condo nodes together) Talapas offers 14,520+ CPU cores, 129 TB of memory, 89 GPUs (A100, H100, and V100), and roughly 3 PB of storage.






NoteCondo Nodes



Research groups can also purchase condo nodes that their members get priority access to—about 166 additional researcher-owned CPU nodes plus V100, A100, and H100 GPUs. If your lab owns condo nodes, your PI can tell you which partition to use. Numbers here come from RACS Services; check the Talapas Knowledge Base for current counts, since the hardware changes as groups buy in.

The PIRG is both your access group and the account your jobs are charged to. Three policies shape where your files should live:

/scratch is purged. Anything in /scratch/<PIRG>/ that has not been accessed in 90 days is deleted automatically, without warning. SLURM (Simple Linux Utility for Resource Management) is the software that manages the cluster [@yoo2003slurm]. It:

Allocates resources fairly among users
Queues jobs when resources are busy
Tracks resource usage

SLURM is the dominant scheduler on academic and national-lab clusters worldwide, so everything in this chapter transfers to almost any cluster you will encounter. Its job is to decide when, where, and with what resources every job runs. The mental model is a request-and-grant transaction:

You declare what your job needs: how many CPU cores, how much memory, how long it will run, and whether it needs a GPU.
SLURM looks across all the nodes, finds one (or several) that can satisfy that request without conflicting with jobs already running there, and reserves those resources for you.
Your job runs on that reserved slice of a compute node. When it finishes, or when it exceeds the limits you declared, SLURM reclaims the resources and hands them to the next job in line.







NoteKey concept: the resource declaration is a contract



You do not take resources on a cluster; you ask for them. SLURM keeps its side of the bargain by giving you exclusive access to the CPUs, memory, and GPUs you declared, and your job must keep its side by not exceeding them. Exceed your declared memory (--mem) and SLURM kills the job with state OUT_OF_MEMORY; exceed your declared wall-clock time (--time) and it is killed with TIMEOUT. Both are hard limits, not warnings. This is why the chapter keeps returning to sizing requests honestly: under-requesting kills jobs, and over-requesting wastes shared capacity and delays your own start.


Every job at UO must also name an account, which is your PIRG. This is how usage is tracked and how fair-share accounting (next section) knows whose turn it is. If you do not know your PIRG, run groups after logging in. You can set it once in your shell profile so you never have to type --account= again:
$ echo 'export SLURM_ACCOUNT=myPIRG'  >> ~/.bash_profile
$ echo 'export SBATCH_ACCOUNT=myPIRG' >> ~/.bash_profile
$ source ~/.bash_profile


A naive scheduler would run jobs first-come, first-served. SLURM does something more equitable: fair-share scheduling. Each job gets a priority that depends in part on how much your PIRG has used the cluster recently. Groups that have consumed a lot of compute in the recent past are nudged down the queue; groups that have used little are nudged up. Over time this balances access so that no single heavy user can monopolize the machine. You can see the factors behind your own jobs’ priority with sprio and your group’s usage with sshare -u $USER.
Fair-share has a practical, almost counterintuitive implication for how you should size your jobs. Because SLURM also tries to fill small gaps in the schedule (a technique called backfill), a small, well-sized job often starts sooner than a large one, even if the large one was submitted first. If you ask for 4 cores and 16 GB for one hour, SLURM can slot you into a gap while a bigger job waits for a whole node to free up. If you ask for a whole node for two days, it has to wait until a node-sized gap opens. The lesson is not to game the queue (you cannot) but to size your jobs honestly to what they need, which both gets you running sooner and leaves resources for everyone else.
QOS (quality of service) limits ride alongside fair-share. A QOS caps how much one user can hold at once, for example a maximum number of simultaneously running jobs or a ceiling on total cores. These limits are why you will sometimes see a job sit in the queue with a reason like QOSMaxCpuPerUserLimit: you have not done anything wrong; you have hit a per-user cap, and earlier jobs must finish before the next one starts. Section 1.8.4 lists the common reasons and what to do about each.




A batch script combines SLURM directives with your commands:
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=my_analysis      # Job name (shows in queue)
#SBATCH --partition=compute         # Partition (queue)
#SBATCH --account=myPIRG            # Your PIRG name
#SBATCH --output=output_%j.log      # Standard output (%j = job ID)
#SBATCH --error=error_%j.log        # Standard error
#SBATCH --time=04:00:00             # Time limit (HH:MM:SS)
#SBATCH --nodes=1                   # Number of nodes
#SBATCH --ntasks-per-node=1         # Tasks per node
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4           # CPUs per task
#SBATCH --mem=16G                   # Memory per node

# Stop on the first error (see below)
set -euo pipefail

# Load required modules (inside the script, after the directives)
module purge
module load R/4.3.3

# Change to working directory
cd /projects/myPIRG/myusername/analysis

# Run your program
Rscript my_analysis.R
Three details in this script deserve emphasis.
The #SBATCH lines are the resource declaration. They must come at the very top, after #!/bin/bash and before any command. To the shell they are comments; to sbatch they are the contract described in Section 1.6. Anything you can write as #SBATCH --flag you can also pass on the command line (sbatch --mem=32G my_script.sh), and the command-line version wins, which is handy for one-off overrides.
set -euo pipefail should be the first real command. This trio of shell options (?@sec-strict-mode) makes the script exit immediately if any command fails (-e), treats unset variables as errors (-u), and makes a pipeline fail if any stage fails rather than only the last (-o pipefail). Without it, a script continues past a failed step: if module load R/4.3.3 fails because the module name changed, the script carries on to Rscript ... with no R loaded and produces a confusing “command not found” (or, worse, silently uses a system R with none of your packages). With it, the script stops at the failed line and the .err log shows exactly where. See ?@sec-shell-scripting for more on these options.
Modules must be loaded inside the script. The environment of your login session does not follow the job to the compute node. A batch job starts on a fresh node with no modules loaded, so module load R on the login node before sbatch accomplishes nothing for the job. This is the most common source of “command not found” errors in first batch jobs; the fix is module purge followed by explicit module load lines inside the script, with version numbers (R/4.3.3, not R) so the job runs the same way next year.

Tip



Request only what you need! Smaller resource requests run sooner (Section 1.6.1). Start with a modest over-estimate, then use seff to right-size the next run (Section 1.9).






Memory: if you specify neither --mem nor --mem-per-cpu, you get roughly 3.7 GB per core (the node’s memory divided by its cores). Ask explicitly for anything more.
Time: the default on compute is the partition maximum (24 hours), which is often too long for small jobs (it makes them harder to backfill) and too short for large ones.
CPUs: --cpus-per-task defaults to 1. Multi-threaded tools (bwa -t, samtools -@, R’s future workers) need more; single-threaded scripts do not, and asking for 8 cores your code cannot use just delays your start.
Partition: none. Every job must name one.

The two reasons that do need intervention are ReqNodeNotAvail, Reserved for maintenance (add --time-min or shorten --time) and AssocGrpCPUMinutesLimit (contact RACS). The Talapas Knowledge Base article Why is my SLURM job not running? covers the rarer cases.



# Cancel specific job
$ scancel 12345678

# Cancel all your jobs
$ scancel -u $USER

# Cancel only your pending (not yet running) jobs
$ scancel -u $USER -t PENDING



After a job completes:
$ seff 12345678
$ sacct -j 12345678 --format=JobID,JobName,ReqMem,MaxRSS,Elapsed,State,ExitCode
seff prints a friendly summary (state, CPU efficiency, memory efficiency, wall-clock time); sacct gives the same facts in tabular form that you can script against. Reading these after every job is the foundation of the next section.




Resource requests pull in two opposite directions, and learning to balance them is the single most valuable HPC skill. On one side, smaller requests run sooner: the backfill scheduler slots small jobs into gaps a large job could never fit, so over-asking for memory or time directly delays your own work. On the other side, you must request enough: exceed --mem and the job dies with OUT_OF_MEMORY; exceed --time and it dies with TIMEOUT, often after hours of progress.
The resolution is empirical. The first time you run a new step, err slightly on the high side so it does not die. Then read seff to see what it really needed, and trim subsequent submissions toward that number with a modest safety margin. Table 8 explains what to look at.

In practice this is a two-submission loop. First run: generous but not absurd limits, for example --mem=32G --time=04:00:00 --cpus-per-task=4 for an unknown step, then seff <jobid> as soon as it finishes. Second and later runs: --mem at MaxRSS × 1.2, --time at Elapsed × 1.2, and --cpus-per-task at whatever the tool actually used. A step that requested 64 GB and used 12 GB has a new request of about 15 GB, a fourfold reduction that noticeably improves its queue position. After one pass through a multi-step pipeline you have an accurate resource profile for every step, and subsequent runs start promptly because each asks only for what it needs.






WarningA finished job is not necessarily a successful job



Before treating a run as done, check two things together: seff reports State: COMPLETED with exit code 0:0, and the output file you expected exists and is complete (for example, the script’s final “Wrote …” message appears in the .out log). A job killed by OUT_OF_MEMORY or TIMEOUT mid-write leaves a truncated file on disk that looks valid but is not, and the next step in your pipeline then fails with a confusing downstream error instead of the real cause.





For testing and development, use interactive jobs instead of batch:
# Start interactive session
$ srun --pty --partition=interactive --account=myPIRG \
       --time=2:00:00 --cpus-per-task=4 --mem=8G /bin/bash
The interactive partition is reserved for exactly this kind of session, with a 12-hour limit; use interactivegpu if you need a GPU to test against.
Your prompt will change from login1 to something like n049, indicating you’re on a compute node.
Interactive jobs are ideal for:

Testing workflows before batch submission
Debugging code
Quick data exploration
Running GUI applications via Open OnDemand

The discipline that goes with them: type exit the moment you are done. An interactive session holds its reserved cores and memory whether or not you are typing, and an idle session is pure waste that someone else could be using. Use an interactive session when you intend to watch the work; use sbatch for anything you intend to walk away from, because a batch job survives your laptop sleeping, your network dropping, and you logging off for the night.



Talapas uses the Lmod module system to manage software. This lets multiple versions coexist without conflicts.


# List available modules
$ module avail

# Search for specific software
$ module spider R
$ module spider python

# Load a module
$ module load R/4.3.3
$ module load miniconda3/20240410

# See loaded modules
$ module list

# Unload a module
$ module unload R

# Reset to default state
$ module purge









Important



Always load modules after the #SBATCH directives in your batch scripts:
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=analysis
#SBATCH --partition=compute
#SBATCH --account=myPIRG
# ... other directives ...

# Load modules here
module load R/4.3.3

# Now run your code
Rscript analysis.R


Modules are loaded per shell. They do not persist between logins, and (as Section 1.7 explained) they do not travel from the login node into a batch job. Specify version numbers (R/4.3.3, not R) so that a default-version change on the cluster cannot silently change your results.
