?@sec-hpc-talapas






The short version: code goes to GitHub (?@sec-git-github), documents go to OneDrive or Dropbox, and big data goes to Talapas (?@sec-talapas-storage). Whatever else you do, keep your raw data somewhere backed up and untouched.



The University pays for a number of software licenses that you can use for free. The UO Software Downloads site at https://software.uoregon.edu (sign in with your Duck ID) offers MATLAB, Mathematica, LabVIEW, SPSS and SPSS Amos, ESRI ArcGIS, and more; some titles need a license code or a connection to the UO network or VPN to activate, and availability can differ between students and employees, so check the site for the current list. The Microsoft 365 desktop apps are installed from https://office.uoregon.edu. For Adobe products, students get Adobe Express on personal devices, while the full Creative Cloud suite is available in campus computer labs. UO-managed computers (as opposed to your personal laptop) install approved software through the Software Center app.
It is worth noticing that none of the tools at the center of this course, the shell, R, Python, Quarto, LaTeX, Git, VS Code, and Positron, require a license at all. They are free and open source, they will follow you to any future institution or employer, and nothing you build with them will stop working when a contract lapses.



You will read hundreds of papers before your qualifying exam, and a reference manager is the only sane way to keep track of them. Zotero (https://www.zotero.org) is free and open source. Its browser connector saves a paper’s citation, and usually the PDF, from a journal page or PubMed with one click; group libraries let you share a reading list with your lab or rotation group; and it inserts citations and bibliographies into Word and into Quarto documents (Insert → Citation in the visual editor). Citing from Quarto is covered in ?@sec-quarto-documents, and a well-kept Zotero library makes it painless. Start now, while the library is small.



UO provides Microsoft Copilot Chat (https://copilot.microsoft.com) as a UO-protected generative AI assistant; sign in with your UO account. UO-supported AI tools are approved for specific data classifications, while unsupported tools are approved for green data only; the current list of tools and what each may be used with is on UO’s AI Service Offerings page. The course policy is simple: you may use AI to help you learn, debug, and get suggestions, but the work you submit must be your own. These tools are excellent at explaining error messages and suggesting code, and confidently wrong surprisingly often, so always read, run, and understand what they produce. We look at AI-assisted coding in depth in ?@sec-ai-assisted-coding.



Research Advanced Computing Services (RACS), at https://racs.uoregon.edu, runs the University’s research computing and supports UO researchers with computing of every kind. Their best-known service is the Talapas HPC cluster, with CPU, GPU, and large-memory nodes and more than 225 scientific software packages installed. Beyond the cluster, RACS provides large-scale research data storage (roughly $35 per terabyte per year) for data that does not fit in what Talapas includes; Globus for fast, reliable transfer of very large datasets, for example from a sequencing core or a collaborator; consulting on software installation, code optimization, data security, and hardware purchases; grant support for the computing and data-management sections of proposals; and help reaching resources beyond UO, including national supercomputers through NSF ACCESS and cloud consulting for AWS and Azure. Contact them at racs@uoregon.edu or through the RACS service desk. They are there to help; ask early.


To understand why a cluster matters, compare it with the laptop you are reading this on. Table 4 puts the numbers side by side.



Table 4: A typical laptop compared with the Talapas cluster

A single standard node has roughly ten times the cores and thirty times the memory of a laptop, and Talapas has hundreds of nodes. Your storage there consists of a 250 GB home directory plus your lab’s project space, 2 TB by default (?@sec-talapas-storage). When an analysis reports “out of memory,” or would take days on your laptop, it is a job for Talapas. As ?@sec-computer-systems explains, memory is usually the binding constraint in data analysis, and the large-memory nodes exist precisely for the assemblies, image stacks, and single-cell matrices that will not fit anywhere else.



Every Talapas user is sponsored by a UO principal investigator and belongs to at least one PIRG (Principal Investigator Research Group), which the PI is responsible for. Ask your PI, or your rotation PI, to add you, and request the account through the Talapas customer portal at https://hpcrcf.atlassian.net/servicedesk/customer/portal/1/group/1/create/9. A PI who does not yet have a PIRG can request one from racs@uoregon.edu. Setup can take a few days, so ask early; for this course, class access will be arranged before the Talapas material in ?@sec-hpc-talapas. The Talapas Knowledge Base is the authoritative documentation.



You do not need to master SSH (?@sec-talapas-ssh) to start using Talapas. Open OnDemand at https://ondemand.talapas.uoregon.edu gives you the cluster through a web browser; log in with your Duck ID using Chrome or Firefox (a private window avoids login glitches). From there you can launch Jupyter Lab notebooks running on Talapas; a full remote desktop with RStudio, MATLAB, and Stata; a shell in the browser; a file explorer for drag-and-drop transfer between your laptop and the cluster; and a job composer for submitting batch jobs. Because OnDemand apps run as jobs on compute nodes, they keep running even after you close your browser, so remember to end sessions you no longer need. Command-line access over SSH and job scheduling with SLURM are covered in ?@sec-hpc-talapas.




This chapter mapped the University’s computing landscape so that you can find your way around it. Key takeaways:

Your Duck ID with Duo unlocks nearly everything; your UO email is your Microsoft 365 and Dropbox sign-in; the VPN is needed only for campus-restricted resources and is recommended but not required for Talapas
Help is available from the Service Portal and Technology Service Desk, UO Libraries Data Services (workshops, consultations, drop-in desk), RACS, and CBDS; a good question includes the exact error, the command, your system, and what you tried
Everyone has Microsoft 365 with 1 TB of OneDrive; UO Dropbox is limited to faculty, staff, and GEs; synced folders have real paths, usually with spaces that must be quoted
Data is green, amber, or red; IRB and HIPAA data are red; only green data may go into unsupported AI tools; encrypt your laptop and de-identify early
Follow the 3-2-1 backup rule and remember that a synced folder is not a backup
Code goes to GitHub, documents to OneDrive/Dropbox, big data to Talapas
UO licenses MATLAB, Mathematica, and more at software.uoregon.edu, but the core tools of this course are free and open source
Zotero manages references; Copilot Chat is UO’s protected AI assistant
RACS runs Talapas (14,500+ cores, ~129 TB RAM, 89 GPUs, ~3 PB storage), provides storage, Globus, consulting, and grant support; every user belongs to a PIRG; Open OnDemand offers Jupyter, RStudio, a shell, and file transfer from a browser

Next, ?@sec-unix-fundamentals opens the terminal and begins the command-line skills that run through the rest of the book.









TipPractice Exercises




Find your synced folder: Sign in to OneDrive (and Dropbox, if you are a GE) with your UO account and install the sync app. From a terminal, cd into the synced folder, run pwd, and write down the absolute path. How did you handle the spaces in the name?
Classify three datasets: For each of the following, state whether it is green, amber, or red data and where you could store it: (a) a table of Young’s modulus measurements from a hydrogel you made; (b) survey responses from human participants under an IRB protocol, including names; (c) the R scripts that made the figures for your last paper.
Set up a backup: Configure Time Machine or File History with an external drive, or verify that your OneDrive folder is syncing. Then delete a test file from a synced folder and try to recover it. Did the recovery work? Would it have worked for a file you overwrote three weeks ago?
Make the 3-2-1 plan: For the most important document you own (a thesis draft, a manuscript, a dataset), list where the three copies are or will be, which two kinds of storage they use, and which copy is off-site.
Start your Talapas account: Ask your PI whether their lab has a PIRG and, if so, to add you. Then log in to Open OnDemand and open the file explorer to look at your home directory. What is the path?

title: Computing Resources at the University of Oregon
text:
Almost everything in this chapter begins with your Duck ID, the UO username and password that you manage at https://duckid.uoregon.edu. It is the key to email, Canvas, Microsoft 365, the software download site, and Talapas. Most UO services also require two-step login through Duo: after entering your password, you approve the login on a second device, usually the Duo Mobile app on your phone. Set Duo up before you need it; being unable to log in to a service you need in a hurry is a frustrating way to discover that your phone is not enrolled.
Your UO email address (you@uoregon.edu) doubles as your sign-in name for Microsoft 365 and for UO’s Dropbox contract. When a service asks you to “sign in with your work or school account,” this is the account it means.
The UO VPN, delivered through the Cisco Secure Client and downloadable from https://uovpn.uoregon.edu, makes your off-campus computer appear to be on the campus network. You only need it for campus-restricted resources such as some library databases, departmental file shares, and some licensed software that must be activated from the campus network. Most UO services, including email, Canvas, Microsoft 365, Teams, and Zoom, work from anywhere without it.






NoteTalapas and the VPN



For Talapas, the VPN is recommended but not required. Without it, connect over SSH to login.talapas.uoregon.edu, which is a load balancer that distributes users across the login nodes; expect Duo prompts. With the VPN active, you may also connect directly to an individual login node, login1 through login4. The mechanics of SSH and job submission are in ?@sec-hpc-talapas.

title: Computing Resources at the University of Oregon
text:
There is a lot of help available at UO, and a large part of getting unstuck quickly is knowing which door to knock on. The UO Service Portal at https://service.uoregon.edu is the front door for all campus technology: it has a searchable knowledge base and a ticketing system, and most questions about accounts, software, Wi-Fi, and cloud storage already have an article there, so search it first. Behind the portal sits the Technology Service Desk, reachable by phone at 541-346-4357 or through live chat.
For data analysis rather than technology, UO Libraries Data Services (https://library.uoregon.edu/data-services) is an underused treasure. They run free workshops on R, Python, data analysis, and related topics; offer one-on-one consultations, in person or on Zoom, on statistics, R, Python, version control, and data-management plans; and staff a drop-in help desk in Knight Library on weekdays from 11am to 4pm.
For research computing, RACS (Research Advanced Computing Services), which runs Talapas, can be reached at racs@uoregon.edu or through their service desk at https://hpcrcf.atlassian.net/servicedesk/customer/portal/1; Section 1.10 describes what they do. Closer to home, the Center for Biomedical Data Science (CBDS) at the Knight Campus, directed by the author of this book, supports the computational and data-science side of biomedical research at the Knight Campus, including training such as this course; ask the instructor about CBDS resources and events. Your home department and the Knight Campus also have IT staff who can help with lab computers and shared storage.


Whoever you ask, the quality of the answer depends on the quality of the question. Start by saying what you were trying to do (“I’m trying to install R on my M2 Mac”), then include the exact error message as copied text, not a blurry photograph of your screen (a screenshot is acceptable only if the text cannot be copied). Show the command or code you ran and what you expected to happen, say what you have already tried (restarted? searched the error? checked your location with pwd?), and state your system: macOS, Windows, or Ubuntu, and the chip type. For code problems, reduce the problem to a minimal example, the smallest piece of code that still shows the failure. Half the time, the discipline of writing a good question leads you to the answer yourself; the other half, it lets someone else answer in a single reply.

title: Computing Resources at the University of Oregon
text:
Every UO student and employee has a Microsoft 365 license, which you access by signing in at https://office.uoregon.edu with your UO email address. Table 1 lists what it includes.



Table 1: The Microsoft 365 tools available to UO students and employees









Tool
What it is for




Outlook
UO email and calendar


Word, Excel, PowerPoint, OneNote
Desktop, web, and mobile apps; install them on your own devices from office.uoregon.edu


Teams
Chat, meetings, and shared files for groups and labs


OneDrive
Your personal cloud storage (1 TB)


SharePoint / Teams files
Shared storage owned by a group rather than a person


Copilot Chat
UO-protected generative AI assistant, when signed in with your UO account








OneDrive is your personal cloud storage, available at no cost with 1 TB of space. The OneDrive sync app for Mac and Windows creates a OneDrive folder on your computer, and files you save there are copied to the cloud automatically, so they survive a lost or dead laptop. You can share files and folders with UO colleagues and with outside collaborators. OneDrive is approved for FERPA and HIPAA data (see Section 1.4), and individual files may be as large as 250 GB.






WarningOneDrive is yours; lab data belongs in shared storage



OneDrive belongs to you, and when you leave UO it goes away. Data that belongs to a lab, such as raw experimental data, shared analysis code, and protocols, should live in storage the lab controls: a Teams/SharePoint site, a lab Dropbox team folder, or the lab’s project space on Talapas. Otherwise, it leaves when you do.





UO also holds an institutional Dropbox contract, but eligibility changed in 2026. Since March 2026, Dropbox accounts under the UO contract are available to faculty, staff, officers of administration, and graduate employees (GEs); students who are not UO employees no longer have access and should use OneDrive instead. If you are eligible, sign in with your UO email address and install the desktop app so that your files sync to a local folder; individual accounts have 2 TB of storage, and labs and departments can purchase team storage. Your lab may also share a Dropbox team folder with you regardless of whether you have your own account. Dropbox is approved for green and amber data, including FERPA records, but not for HIPAA or other red data.



Both OneDrive and Dropbox create an ordinary folder on your computer, which means it has a path you can use from the command line and from your scripts. Typical locations look like these (yours may differ slightly):
# macOS
~/Library/CloudStorage/OneDrive-UniversityofOregon
~/University\ of\ Oregon\ Dropbox/Your\ Name

# Windows, as seen from Ubuntu/WSL
/mnt/c/Users/you/OneDrive\ -\ University\ of\ Oregon
Notice the backslashes: names such as University of Oregon Dropbox contain spaces, and the shell uses spaces to separate arguments, so a path with spaces must be quoted (cd "University of Oregon Dropbox") or escaped with backslashes. Tab completion adds the escapes for you, and ?@sec-unix-fundamentals has more on paths and quoting. Find your own synced folder with cd, ls, and Tab completion. Synced folders are excellent for documents and drafts, but large or rapidly changing analysis files are better kept on local disk or on Talapas, where the sync client cannot interfere with them.

title: Computing Resources at the University of Oregon
text:
UO classifies data by the harm that would result if it were exposed, and the classification determines where it may be stored and which tools may touch it. Know the class of your data before you choose where to put it. Table 2 summarizes the three classes.



Table 2: UO’s data classification and where each class may live










Class
Examples
May be stored in




Green (low risk)
Published data, your code, most de-identified research data
Almost anywhere, including AI tools


Amber (medium risk)
FERPA student records, unpublished research data
OneDrive, Dropbox, Teams/SharePoint


Red (high risk)
HIPAA / protected health information, Social Security numbers, credit-card numbers
Only approved systems (for example OneDrive for HIPAA); ask first












Important



Only green data may be entered into AI tools that UO does not officially support. Microsoft Copilot Chat, signed in with your UO account, is approved for more; see Section 1.9.




Two categories deserve special attention. Human-subjects data, meaning anything covered by an Institutional Review Board (IRB) protocol, and protected health information covered by HIPAA are red, high-risk data. Store them only where your IRB protocol and UO approve: UO OneDrive and Teams are approved for HIPAA data, Dropbox is not, and personal cloud accounts (a personal Google Drive or iCloud), email attachments, and unsupported AI tools are never acceptable. De-identify data as early in the workflow as you can, and keep the key that links identifiers to participants separately and securely. Encrypt your laptop (FileVault on macOS, BitLocker or Device Encryption on Windows) and use a screen lock, so that a stolen backpack is an inconvenience rather than a breach. Finally, remember that unpublished data and code are valuable; do not post them publicly until your PI agrees. When in doubt, ask before you store or share, whether your PI, the IRB, or the Service Portal. It is far easier than cleaning up afterwards.

title: Computing Resources at the University of Oregon
text:
Every year, someone loses a thesis chapter to a dead laptop or a stolen bag. The standard defense is the 3-2-1 rule: keep three copies of anything important, on two different kinds of storage, with one copy off-site. In practice that might mean the working copy on your laptop, a versioned backup on an external drive using Time Machine (macOS) or File History (Windows), and an off-site copy in OneDrive or your lab’s Dropbox or server. For code, GitHub adds a fourth layer: every commit you push is a backup with full history (?@sec-git-github).






WarningA synced folder is not a backup



OneDrive and Dropbox protect you against a dead laptop, but not against yourself. If you delete or overwrite a file, the deletion syncs everywhere within seconds. Keep versioned backups (Time Machine, File History, Git) in addition to sync, and test that you can restore a file before the day you need to.

text:
With several storage options available, it helps to have a rule of thumb. Table 3 summarizes what each is good for.

The short version: code goes to GitHub (?@sec-git-github), documents go to OneDrive or Dropbox, and big data goes to Talapas (?@sec-talapas-storage). Whatever else you do, keep your raw data somewhere backed up and untouched.

title: Computing Resources at the University of Oregon
text:
The University pays for a number of software licenses that you can use for free. The UO Software Downloads site at https://software.uoregon.edu (sign in with your Duck ID) offers MATLAB, Mathematica, LabVIEW, SPSS and SPSS Amos, ESRI ArcGIS, and more; some titles need a license code or a connection to the UO network or VPN to activate, and availability can differ between students and employees, so check the site for the current list. The Microsoft 365 desktop apps are installed from https://office.uoregon.edu. For Adobe products, students get Adobe Express on personal devices, while the full Creative Cloud suite is available in campus computer labs. UO-managed computers (as opposed to your personal laptop) install approved software through the Software Center app.
It is worth noticing that none of the tools at the center of this course, the shell, R, Python, Quarto, LaTeX, Git, VS Code, and Positron, require a license at all. They are free and open source, they will follow you to any future institution or employer, and nothing you build with them will stop working when a contract lapses.

title: Computing Resources at the University of Oregon
text: You will read hundreds of papers before your qualifying exam, and a reference manager is the only sane way to keep track of them. Zotero (https://www.zotero.org) is free and open source. Its browser connector saves a paper’s citation, and usually the PDF, from a journal page or PubMed with one click; group libraries let you share a reading list with your lab or rotation group; and it inserts citations and bibliographies into Word and into Quarto documents (Insert → Citation in the visual editor). Citing from Quarto is covered in ?@sec-quarto-documents, and a well-kept Zotero library makes it painless. Start now, while the library is small.

title: Computing Resources at the University of Oregon
text: UO provides Microsoft Copilot Chat (https://copilot.microsoft.com) as a UO-protected generative AI assistant; sign in with your UO account. UO-supported AI tools are approved for specific data classifications, while unsupported tools are approved for green data only; the current list of tools and what each may be used with is on UO’s AI Service Offerings page. The course policy is simple: you may use AI to help you learn, debug, and get suggestions, but the work you submit must be your own. These tools are excellent at explaining error messages and suggesting code, and confidently wrong surprisingly often, so always read, run, and understand what they produce. We look at AI-assisted coding in depth in ?@sec-ai-assisted-coding.

title: Computing Resources at the University of Oregon
text:
Research Advanced Computing Services (RACS), at https://racs.uoregon.edu, runs the University’s research computing and supports UO researchers with computing of every kind. Their best-known service is the Talapas HPC cluster, with CPU, GPU, and large-memory nodes and more than 225 scientific software packages installed. Beyond the cluster, RACS provides large-scale research data storage (roughly $35 per terabyte per year) for data that does not fit in what Talapas includes; Globus for fast, reliable transfer of very large datasets, for example from a sequencing core or a collaborator; consulting on software installation, code optimization, data security, and hardware purchases; grant support for the computing and data-management sections of proposals; and help reaching resources beyond UO, including national supercomputers through NSF ACCESS and cloud consulting for AWS and Azure. Contact them at racs@uoregon.edu or through the RACS service desk. They are there to help; ask early.


To understand why a cluster matters, compare it with the laptop you are reading this on. Table 4 puts the numbers side by side.

A single standard node has roughly ten times the cores and thirty times the memory of a laptop, and Talapas has hundreds of nodes. Your storage there consists of a 250 GB home directory plus your lab’s project space, 2 TB by default (?@sec-talapas-storage). When an analysis reports “out of memory,” or would take days on your laptop, it is a job for Talapas. As ?@sec-computer-systems explains, memory is usually the binding constraint in data analysis, and the large-memory nodes exist precisely for the assemblies, image stacks, and single-cell matrices that will not fit anywhere else.



Every Talapas user is sponsored by a UO principal investigator and belongs to at least one PIRG (Principal Investigator Research Group), which the PI is responsible for. Ask your PI, or your rotation PI, to add you, and request the account through the Talapas customer portal at https://hpcrcf.atlassian.net/servicedesk/customer/portal/1/group/1/create/9. A PI who does not yet have a PIRG can request one from racs@uoregon.edu. Setup can take a few days, so ask early; for this course, class access will be arranged before the Talapas material in ?@sec-hpc-talapas. The Talapas Knowledge Base is the authoritative documentation.



You do not need to master SSH (?@sec-talapas-ssh) to start using Talapas. Open OnDemand at https://ondemand.talapas.uoregon.edu gives you the cluster through a web browser; log in with your Duck ID using Chrome or Firefox (a private window avoids login glitches). From there you can launch Jupyter Lab notebooks running on Talapas; a full remote desktop with RStudio, MATLAB, and Stata; a shell in the browser; a file explorer for drag-and-drop transfer between your laptop and the cluster; and a job composer for submitting batch jobs. Because OnDemand apps run as jobs on compute nodes, they keep running even after you close your browser, so remember to end sessions you no longer need. Command-line access over SSH and job scheduling with SLURM are covered in ?@sec-hpc-talapas.

title: Computing Resources at the University of Oregon
text:
This chapter mapped the University’s computing landscape so that you can find your way around it. Key takeaways:

Your Duck ID with Duo unlocks nearly everything; your UO email is your Microsoft 365 and Dropbox sign-in; the VPN is needed only for campus-restricted resources and is recommended but not required for Talapas
Help is available from the Service Portal and Technology Service Desk, UO Libraries Data Services (workshops, consultations, drop-in desk), RACS, and CBDS; a good question includes the exact error, the command, your system, and what you tried
Everyone has Microsoft 365 with 1 TB of OneDrive; UO Dropbox is limited to faculty, staff, and GEs; synced folders have real paths, usually with spaces that must be quoted
Data is green, amber, or red; IRB and HIPAA data are red; only green data may go into unsupported AI tools; encrypt your laptop and de-identify early
Follow the 3-2-1 backup rule and remember that a synced folder is not a backup
Code goes to GitHub, documents to OneDrive/Dropbox, big data to Talapas
UO licenses MATLAB, Mathematica, and more at software.uoregon.edu, but the core tools of this course are free and open source
Zotero manages references; Copilot Chat is UO’s protected AI assistant
RACS runs Talapas (14,500+ cores, ~129 TB RAM, 89 GPUs, ~3 PB storage), provides storage, Globus, consulting, and grant support; every user belongs to a PIRG; Open OnDemand offers Jupyter, RStudio, a shell, and file transfer from a browser

Next, ?@sec-unix-fundamentals opens the terminal and begins the command-line skills that run through the rest of the book.

title: Computing Resources at the University of Oregon
text:
TipPractice Exercises




Find your synced folder: Sign in to OneDrive (and Dropbox, if you are a GE) with your UO account and install the sync app. From a terminal, cd into the synced folder, run pwd, and write down the absolute path. How did you handle the spaces in the name?
Classify three datasets: For each of the following, state whether it is green, amber, or red data and where you could store it: (a) a table of Young’s modulus measurements from a hydrogel you made; (b) survey responses from human participants under an IRB protocol, including names; (c) the R scripts that made the figures for your last paper.
Set up a backup: Configure Time Machine or File History with an external drive, or verify that your OneDrive folder is syncing. Then delete a test file from a synced folder and try to recover it. Did the recovery work? Would it have worked for a file you overwrote three weeks ago?
Make the 3-2-1 plan: For the most important document you own (a thesis draft, a manuscript, a dataset), list where the three copies are or will be, which two kinds of storage they use, and which copy is off-site.

title: Introduction to Computational Tools
text:
NoteLearning Objectives



After completing this chapter, you will be able to:

Articulate why computational skills are essential for modern bioscience research
Distinguish between coding and scripting languages
Identify the computational tools covered in this course
Set up your computing environment for the course





Modern biological research has undergone a profound transformation. The advent of high-throughput technologies—from next-generation sequencing to automated microscopy to mass spectrometry—has generated an explosion of data that far exceeds what can be analyzed manually. Consider these examples:

A single human genome sequence contains approximately 6 billion base pairs
A typical RNA-seq experiment generates tens of millions of short reads
Proteomics studies can identify and quantify thousands of proteins simultaneously
High-content imaging screens produce terabytes of image data

To make sense of this data deluge, researchers must be fluent in computational tools. This fluency goes beyond simply running pre-made software—it requires understanding how to manipulate data, automate analyses, and ensure reproducibility.



There are compelling reasons to invest time in developing computational proficiency:
Speed and Scale. Computational tools allow you to perform thousands of operations with single commands. Tasks that would take days by hand can be completed in seconds.
Reproducibility. Scripts and code serve as a complete record of your analysis. Unlike clicking through graphical interfaces, command-line workflows can be exactly reproduced, shared, and verified [@sandve2013ten; @wilson2017good].
Flexibility. General-purpose programming languages can handle virtually any data format or analysis type. You’re not limited to what software developers anticipated.
Access to Specialized Tools. Many cutting-edge analysis tools in bioinformatics are only available through the command line. Learning to use the shell opens doors to thousands of free programs developed by scientists for scientists.
High-Performance Computing. Large-scale analyses require computing clusters. These systems are accessed and controlled through command-line interfaces.






TipCareer Impact



Computational skills are increasingly valued in academic and industry positions. Investing in these skills now will pay dividends throughout your career. Organizing your computational projects well from the start saves countless hours later [@noble2009quick].





You’ll often hear the terms “coding” and “scripting” used interchangeably, but there are technical distinctions worth understanding.


Compiled languages require a separate compilation step that translates human-readable source code into machine code before execution. Examples include:

C/C++
Fortran
Rust
Go

The compilation process produces optimized executable files that run very quickly. However, compiled languages typically require more setup and are less forgiving of errors during development.



Interpreted languages (or scripting languages) execute code line-by-line at runtime, without a separate compilation step. Examples include:

Bash/Shell
Python
R
Julia
Perl

Interpreted languages offer greater flexibility and faster development cycles at the cost of some execution speed. They’re ideal for data analysis, automation, and interactive exploration.






Note



The distinction between compiled and interpreted languages has become increasingly blurred. Modern systems like Julia use just-in-time (JIT) compilation to achieve near-compiled performance with scripting-language convenience. Python and R can also interface with compiled C/C++ code for performance-critical operations.





For most biological research, interpreted languages are the right choice. They enable rapid prototyping and experimentation—you can try an idea, see if it works, and refine it immediately. Their interactive nature makes them ideal for data exploration, allowing you to probe your data and understand its structure before committing to a particular analysis approach. The scientific computing community has developed extensive libraries for these languages, from statistical methods to machine learning to bioinformatics pipelines. And because interpreted languages tend to have more forgiving syntax and immediate feedback, they present lower barriers to entry for beginners.
In this course, we work primarily with Bash (the Unix shell) and R, with Python installed and used alongside them, and with exposure to high-performance computing concepts that may eventually lead you to compiled languages if your research requires it.




This book and accompanying course introduce you to a carefully selected set of tools that form the foundation of computational research in the life sciences [@buffalo2015bioinformatics].


The Unix shell (specifically Bash) provides a powerful interface for file manipulation that goes far beyond what graphical file managers offer. It includes specialized tools for processing large text-based data files—essential when working with genomic sequences, tabular data, or log files. Perhaps most importantly, the shell lets you combine simple programs into complex workflows through pipes and scripting, and it provides access to remote computing systems using the same commands you use locally. Understanding Unix is essential because it underlies most scientific computing infrastructure, from laptops to supercomputers. The shell is introduced in ?@sec-unix-fundamentals and developed through ?@sec-shell-scripting.



R is a programming language and environment specifically designed for statistical computing and graphics [@rproject2024]. It provides comprehensive statistical analysis capabilities, from basic descriptive statistics to advanced machine learning algorithms. R excels at producing publication-quality graphics with fine-grained control over every visual element. The community has developed thousands of packages for specialized analyses in virtually every domain of science, and R integrates seamlessly with reproducible document systems like Quarto and R Markdown. The RStudio IDE provides an excellent development environment that makes working with R accessible and productive. R is introduced in ?@sec-r-programming, with data wrangling and graphics in ?@sec-tidy-data and ?@sec-data-viz.



Python is a general-purpose programming language that has become the lingua franca of image analysis, machine learning, and instrument control, and it is the language you are most likely to meet in code written by engineers outside the statistics community. R remains the primary language of this course, but Python gets a chapter of its own: you will install it in ?@sec-toolkit, and ?@sec-python-programming covers the language, NumPy, pandas, and plotting at the same depth as ?@sec-r-programming, ending with a translation table between the two. You will also run Python code chunks in Quarto documents (?@sec-quarto-documents) and use Python environments (venv, uv, and conda) both on your laptop and on Talapas. The concepts you learn in Bash and R (variables, loops, functions, files) transfer directly, and many students find that once R is comfortable, Python follows quickly.



All of the code in this course lives in plain-text files, and you will spend most of your working hours in the program that edits them. An integrated development environment (IDE) bundles a text editor with a terminal, a console for interactive R or Python, a file explorer, and a front-end to version control. We use three: VS Code, a general-purpose editor with the largest extension ecosystem; Positron, Posit’s data-science IDE built on the same open-source core as VS Code with R and Python built in; and RStudio, the classic R environment. ?@sec-toolkit walks through installing and using each one and offers guidance on which to choose for which task.



Quarto is an open-source scientific publishing system [@quarto2024] that enables you to combine narrative text with executable code in a single document. From this unified source, you can generate reports, presentations, websites, and books—all while ensuring your analyses are fully reproducible. Because the code runs when the document renders, results always match the code that produced them. You can then share your work in multiple formats (HTML, PDF, Word) without maintaining separate versions. This book itself was written using Quarto! See ?@sec-quarto-documents.



Git is a version control system that tracks changes to your files over time [@chacon2014pro; @blischak2016practical]. GitHub is a web-based platform for hosting Git repositories. Together, they provide a complete history of your project’s development, allowing you to understand how your work evolved and revert to earlier versions if needed. Git enables safe experimentation with new ideas through branching—you can try risky changes without affecting your working code. The platform facilitates collaboration with colleagues worldwide, letting multiple people work on the same project simultaneously. And GitHub makes it easy to share code and data publicly, contributing to open science and reproducible research. Git and GitHub are covered in ?@sec-git-github, with a command reference in ?@sec-appendix-git.



Talapas is the University of Oregon’s computing cluster. You’ll learn to access and navigate this remote computing environment, submit and manage batch jobs that run when resources become available, use software modules to access specialized tools, and scale your analyses far beyond what your laptop can handle. When your analysis takes hours or days, or requires more memory than your personal computer has, Talapas provides the computational power you need (?@sec-hpc-talapas).




Before diving into the technical content, you’ll need to set up your computing environment. This section covers the operating-system level: getting a Unix shell on macOS, Linux, or Windows. The rest of the toolkit (R, Python, Quarto and TinyTeX, VS Code, and Positron) is installed in ?@sec-toolkit, which also has a verification checkpoint and a troubleshooting table; Git is installed in ?@sec-git-github.


macOS is built on a Unix operating system, so a shell is already there. Open Terminal (in Applications → Utilities, or press Cmd-Space and type “Terminal”); if you prefer a more feature-rich terminal, iTerm2 is a popular alternative. One extra step is needed: install Apple’s command-line developer tools, which provide the compilers and Git that many other tools depend on. In Terminal, type
xcode-select --install
and click Install in the dialog that appears. It can take a while; if the command reports that the tools are already installed, you are done.



Linux systems include multiple terminal applications. Open your distribution’s default terminal emulator, often called “Terminal” or “Console” (frequently Ctrl-Alt-T).



Windows requires additional setup to access a Unix-like environment. The recommended approach uses Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL), which runs a real Ubuntu Linux inside Windows. It requires Windows 11 or an up-to-date Windows 10.






CautionWindows Users: Additional Steps Required



Follow these steps to install Ubuntu on Windows:

Right-click Windows PowerShell and choose Run as administrator
Type wsl --install and press Enter. This installs WSL and Ubuntu; there is no separate Ubuntu download
When it finishes, restart your computer
Open Ubuntu from the Start menu and wait while it finishes installing
Create a Linux username and password. They do not need to match your Windows login, but remember them. When you type the password, nothing appears on screen; that is normal, so type it and press Enter
Update Ubuntu’s software (you will be asked for your Linux password):

sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade -y


After this, your Linux home directory is /home/yourname, and your Windows files are visible from Ubuntu at /mnt/c/Users/<name> (for example /mnt/c/Users/<name>/Documents). Having two operating systems on one laptop is confusing at first; ?@sec-toolkit has a “which side am I on?” table (?@tbl-which-side) explaining where to type shell commands (Ubuntu) and where to install R, Python, and the IDEs (Windows). A detailed guide is available at ubuntu.com/tutorials/install-ubuntu-on-wsl2-on-windows-10.



To use the university’s computing cluster, you must be a member of a PIRG (Principal Investigator Research Group), which your PI requests and manages; your login credentials are your Duck ID and password, with Duo two-step login. The UO VPN is recommended but not required: without it, you connect to login.talapas.uoregon.edu, a load balancer that spreads users across the login nodes; with it, you may also connect to a specific login node (login1 through login4) directly. ?@sec-computing-at-uo explains accounts, PIRGs, and the browser-based Open OnDemand interface, and ?@sec-hpc-talapas covers SSH and job submission in detail.

title: Introduction to Computational Tools
text:
Modern biological research has undergone a profound transformation. The advent of high-throughput technologies—from next-generation sequencing to automated microscopy to mass spectrometry—has generated an explosion of data that far exceeds what can be analyzed manually. Consider these examples:

A single human genome sequence contains approximately 6 billion base pairs
A typical RNA-seq experiment generates tens of millions of short reads
Proteomics studies can identify and quantify thousands of proteins simultaneously
High-content imaging screens produce terabytes of image data

To make sense of this data deluge, researchers must be fluent in computational tools. This fluency goes beyond simply running pre-made software—it requires understanding how to manipulate data, automate analyses, and ensure reproducibility.

title: Introduction to Computational Tools
text:
There are compelling reasons to invest time in developing computational proficiency:
Speed and Scale. Computational tools allow you to perform thousands of operations with single commands. Tasks that would take days by hand can be completed in seconds.
Reproducibility. Scripts and code serve as a complete record of your analysis. Unlike clicking through graphical interfaces, command-line workflows can be exactly reproduced, shared, and verified [@sandve2013ten; @wilson2017good].
Flexibility. General-purpose programming languages can handle virtually any data format or analysis type. You’re not limited to what software developers anticipated.
Access to Specialized Tools. Many cutting-edge analysis tools in bioinformatics are only available through the command line. Learning to use the shell opens doors to thousands of free programs developed by scientists for scientists.
High-Performance Computing. Large-scale analyses require computing clusters. These systems are accessed and controlled through command-line interfaces.






TipCareer Impact



Computational skills are increasingly valued in academic and industry positions. Investing in these skills now will pay dividends throughout your career. Organizing your computational projects well from the start saves countless hours later [@noble2009quick].

title: Introduction to Computational Tools
text:
You’ll often hear the terms “coding” and “scripting” used interchangeably, but there are technical distinctions worth understanding.


Compiled languages require a separate compilation step that translates human-readable source code into machine code before execution. Examples include:

C/C++
Fortran
Rust
Go

The compilation process produces optimized executable files that run very quickly. However, compiled languages typically require more setup and are less forgiving of errors during development.



Interpreted languages (or scripting languages) execute code line-by-line at runtime, without a separate compilation step. Examples include:

Bash/Shell
Python
R
Julia
Perl

Interpreted languages offer greater flexibility and faster development cycles at the cost of some execution speed. They’re ideal for data analysis, automation, and interactive exploration.






Note



The distinction between compiled and interpreted languages has become increasingly blurred. Modern systems like Julia use just-in-time (JIT) compilation to achieve near-compiled performance with scripting-language convenience. Python and R can also interface with compiled C/C++ code for performance-critical operations.





For most biological research, interpreted languages are the right choice. They enable rapid prototyping and experimentation—you can try an idea, see if it works, and refine it immediately. Their interactive nature makes them ideal for data exploration, allowing you to probe your data and understand its structure before committing to a particular analysis approach. The scientific computing community has developed extensive libraries for these languages, from statistical methods to machine learning to bioinformatics pipelines. And because interpreted languages tend to have more forgiving syntax and immediate feedback, they present lower barriers to entry for beginners.
In this course, we work primarily with Bash (the Unix shell) and R, with Python installed and used alongside them, and with exposure to high-performance computing concepts that may eventually lead you to compiled languages if your research requires it.

title: Introduction to Computational Tools
text:
This book and accompanying course introduce you to a carefully selected set of tools that form the foundation of computational research in the life sciences [@buffalo2015bioinformatics].


The Unix shell (specifically Bash) provides a powerful interface for file manipulation that goes far beyond what graphical file managers offer. It includes specialized tools for processing large text-based data files—essential when working with genomic sequences, tabular data, or log files. Perhaps most importantly, the shell lets you combine simple programs into complex workflows through pipes and scripting, and it provides access to remote computing systems using the same commands you use locally. Understanding Unix is essential because it underlies most scientific computing infrastructure, from laptops to supercomputers. The shell is introduced in ?@sec-unix-fundamentals and developed through ?@sec-shell-scripting.



R is a programming language and environment specifically designed for statistical computing and graphics [@rproject2024]. It provides comprehensive statistical analysis capabilities, from basic descriptive statistics to advanced machine learning algorithms. R excels at producing publication-quality graphics with fine-grained control over every visual element. The community has developed thousands of packages for specialized analyses in virtually every domain of science, and R integrates seamlessly with reproducible document systems like Quarto and R Markdown. The RStudio IDE provides an excellent development environment that makes working with R accessible and productive. R is introduced in ?@sec-r-programming, with data wrangling and graphics in ?@sec-tidy-data and ?@sec-data-viz.



Python is a general-purpose programming language that has become the lingua franca of image analysis, machine learning, and instrument control, and it is the language you are most likely to meet in code written by engineers outside the statistics community. R remains the primary language of this course, but Python gets a chapter of its own: you will install it in ?@sec-toolkit, and ?@sec-python-programming covers the language, NumPy, pandas, and plotting at the same depth as ?@sec-r-programming, ending with a translation table between the two. You will also run Python code chunks in Quarto documents (?@sec-quarto-documents) and use Python environments (venv, uv, and conda) both on your laptop and on Talapas. The concepts you learn in Bash and R (variables, loops, functions, files) transfer directly, and many students find that once R is comfortable, Python follows quickly.



All of the code in this course lives in plain-text files, and you will spend most of your working hours in the program that edits them. An integrated development environment (IDE) bundles a text editor with a terminal, a console for interactive R or Python, a file explorer, and a front-end to version control. We use three: VS Code, a general-purpose editor with the largest extension ecosystem; Positron, Posit’s data-science IDE built on the same open-source core as VS Code with R and Python built in; and RStudio, the classic R environment. ?@sec-toolkit walks through installing and using each one and offers guidance on which to choose for which task.



Quarto is an open-source scientific publishing system [@quarto2024] that enables you to combine narrative text with executable code in a single document. From this unified source, you can generate reports, presentations, websites, and books—all while ensuring your analyses are fully reproducible. Because the code runs when the document renders, results always match the code that produced them. You can then share your work in multiple formats (HTML, PDF, Word) without maintaining separate versions. This book itself was written using Quarto! See ?@sec-quarto-documents.



Git is a version control system that tracks changes to your files over time [@chacon2014pro; @blischak2016practical]. GitHub is a web-based platform for hosting Git repositories. Together, they provide a complete history of your project’s development, allowing you to understand how your work evolved and revert to earlier versions if needed. Git enables safe experimentation with new ideas through branching—you can try risky changes without affecting your working code. The platform facilitates collaboration with colleagues worldwide, letting multiple people work on the same project simultaneously. And GitHub makes it easy to share code and data publicly, contributing to open science and reproducible research. Git and GitHub are covered in ?@sec-git-github, with a command reference in ?@sec-appendix-git.



Talapas is the University of Oregon’s computing cluster. You’ll learn to access and navigate this remote computing environment, submit and manage batch jobs that run when resources become available, use software modules to access specialized tools, and scale your analyses far beyond what your laptop can handle. When your analysis takes hours or days, or requires more memory than your personal computer has, Talapas provides the computational power you need (?@sec-hpc-talapas).

title: Introduction to Computational Tools
text:
Before diving into the technical content, you’ll need to set up your computing environment. This section covers the operating-system level: getting a Unix shell on macOS, Linux, or Windows. The rest of the toolkit (R, Python, Quarto and TinyTeX, VS Code, and Positron) is installed in ?@sec-toolkit, which also has a verification checkpoint and a troubleshooting table; Git is installed in ?@sec-git-github.


macOS is built on a Unix operating system, so a shell is already there. Open Terminal (in Applications → Utilities, or press Cmd-Space and type “Terminal”); if you prefer a more feature-rich terminal, iTerm2 is a popular alternative. One extra step is needed: install Apple’s command-line developer tools, which provide the compilers and Git that many other tools depend on. In Terminal, type
xcode-select --install
and click Install in the dialog that appears. It can take a while; if the command reports that the tools are already installed, you are done.



Linux systems include multiple terminal applications. Open your distribution’s default terminal emulator, often called “Terminal” or “Console” (frequently Ctrl-Alt-T).



Windows requires additional setup to access a Unix-like environment. The recommended approach uses Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL), which runs a real Ubuntu Linux inside Windows. It requires Windows 11 or an up-to-date Windows 10.






CautionWindows Users: Additional Steps Required



Follow these steps to install Ubuntu on Windows:

Right-click Windows PowerShell and choose Run as administrator
Type wsl --install and press Enter. This installs WSL and Ubuntu; there is no separate Ubuntu download
When it finishes, restart your computer
Open Ubuntu from the Start menu and wait while it finishes installing
Create a Linux username and password. They do not need to match your Windows login, but remember them. When you type the password, nothing appears on screen; that is normal, so type it and press Enter
Update Ubuntu’s software (you will be asked for your Linux password):

sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade -y


After this, your Linux home directory is /home/yourname, and your Windows files are visible from Ubuntu at /mnt/c/Users/<name> (for example /mnt/c/Users/<name>/Documents). Having two operating systems on one laptop is confusing at first; ?@sec-toolkit has a “which side am I on?” table (?@tbl-which-side) explaining where to type shell commands (Ubuntu) and where to install R, Python, and the IDEs (Windows). A detailed guide is available at ubuntu.com/tutorials/install-ubuntu-on-wsl2-on-windows-10.



To use the university’s computing cluster, you must be a member of a PIRG (Principal Investigator Research Group), which your PI requests and manages; your login credentials are your Duck ID and password, with Duo two-step login. The UO VPN is recommended but not required: without it, you connect to login.talapas.uoregon.edu, a load balancer that spreads users across the login nodes; with it, you may also connect to a specific login node (login1 through login4) directly. ?@sec-computing-at-uo explains accounts, PIRGs, and the browser-based Open OnDemand interface, and ?@sec-hpc-talapas covers SSH and job submission in detail.

title: LaTeX Command Reference
Common Data Formats & Public Repositories
text:
This appendix is a field guide to the file formats you will meet most often as a bioengineer working with data, and to the public repositories where published datasets, sequences, genomes, and structures live. It is meant to be scanned in about 15 minutes and returned to whenever you open an unfamiliar file or need to find a published dataset.






Note



Why an appendix and not a tutorial? Recognizing file formats and navigating data repositories is a skill more than a procedure: every repository’s interface evolves, and the right portal depends on your question. The command-line tools used here (head, zcat, grep, wc, wget) are introduced in ?@sec-unix-fundamentals and Lectures 03-05; see ?@sec-grep-regex for more grep. Terms are defined in the the Glossary (?@sec-appendix-glossary).

title: Common Data Formats & Public Repositories
text:
Plain-text tables: CSV and TSV
The workhorse of scientific data exchange. Each line is a row; columns are separated by commas (CSV, .csv) or tab characters (TSV, .tsv or .txt).
sample_id,material,stiffness_kPa,temp_C
S01,PEG_hydrogel,12.4,37
S02,PEG_hydrogel,13.1,37
S03,alginate,8.7,37

The first line is usually a header with column names.
Follow tidy data conventions (Lecture 03): one variable per column, one observation per row, one value per cell.
TSV is safer when text fields might contain commas (e.g., gene descriptions).
Read in R with readr::read_csv() / read_tsv(); in Python with pandas.read_csv() (add sep="\t" for TSV).
Quick shell checks: head file.csv, wc -l file.csv (rows + header), cut -d, -f3 file.csv | sort | uniq -c (tabulate column 3).

title: Common Data Formats & Public Repositories
text:
Spreadsheets: Excel (.xlsx) and its caveats
Excel is fine for viewing and data entry, but it is risky as the only copy of your data:

Automatic conversion: Excel silently converts some values. Gene symbols such as SEPT2, MARCH1, and DEC1 have been turned into dates (“2-Sep”, “1-Mar”), and long numeric IDs are converted to scientific notation, losing digits. A 2016 survey found these errors in roughly one-fifth of papers with supplementary Excel gene lists (Ziemann et al., Genome Biology, https://doi.org/10.1186/s13059-016-1044-7); HGNC later renamed several genes partly because of this. Keeping raw data in plain text and doing all manipulation in code is one of the core recommendations of “good enough” scientific computing practice [@wilson2017good].
Hidden structure: merged cells, colors used as data, multiple tables per sheet, and formulas make files hard to read programmatically.
Proprietary binary format: .xlsx is a zipped XML bundle, so Git cannot show meaningful diffs.







Tip



Keep a CSV copy. Treat raw data as read-only, store a plain-text CSV (one sheet = one CSV) alongside any .xlsx, and do analysis in code. If you must import into Excel, use Data → From Text/CSV and set gene-name or ID columns to Text. In R, readxl::read_excel() reads .xlsx directly without Excel.

title: Common Data Formats & Public Repositories
text:
Sequences: FASTA
Plain text for DNA, RNA, or protein sequences. Each record is a header line starting with > followed by one or more lines of sequence:
>NM_000546.6 Homo sapiens tumor protein p53 (TP53), mRNA
CTCAAAAGTCTAGAGCCACCGTCCAGGGAGCAGGTAGCTGCTGGGCTCCGGGGACACTTTGCGTTCGGGC
TGGGAGCGTGCTTTCCACGACGGTGACACGCTTCCCTGGATTGGCAGCCAGACTGCCTTCCGGGTCACTG
>sp|P04637|P53_HUMAN Cellular tumor antigen p53
MEEPQSDPSVEPPLSQETFSDLWKLLPENNVLSPLPSQAMDDLMLSPDDIEQWFTEDPGP

Extensions: .fa, .fasta, .fna (nucleotide), .faa (amino acid), often gzipped (.fa.gz).
Used for reference genomes, transcripts, primers, and protein sequences.
No quality scores (contrast with FASTQ).
Count records: grep -c '>' file.fasta. List headers: grep '>' file.fasta | head.

title: Common Data Formats & Public Repositories
text:
Raw sequencing reads: FASTQ
Plain text with a strict 4-line-per-read structure (Table 1):
@SRR12345.1 NS500126:1:H7TG3BGXY:1:11101:18923:1057
NCATGCAGCGTACGGTAATTGGCAGGCATTAGCAGCATCC
+
#AAAAFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF



Table 1: The four lines of a FASTQ record









Line
Content




1
Header: read ID plus instrument, run, lane, tile, and x/y position. Starts with @


2
The sequence (A/C/G/T/N)


3
A + separator (sometimes repeats the header)


4
Per-base quality scores, one ASCII character per base, same length as line 2












NoteKey concept - Phred quality scores



Each quality character encodes a Phred score \(Q = -10 \log_{10}(P)\), where \(P\) is the probability that the base call is wrong (Table 2):



Table 2: Phred quality scores and the base-call accuracy they encode





Phred Q
Error probability
Base-call accuracy




10
1 in 10
90%


20
1 in 100
99%


30
1 in 1,000
99.9%


40
1 in 10,000
99.99%






Modern Illumina data use Phred+33 encoding: the character’s ASCII code minus 33 gives Q. So ! (ASCII 33) is Q0, + (43) is Q10, 5 (53) is Q20, ? (63) is Q30, and I (73) is Q40. In the example above, the leading # (Q2) on the N base signals a very low-confidence call.



Paired-end runs produce two files per sample, typically ..._R1_001.fastq.gz and ..._R2_001.fastq.gz; the reads in each file are in the same order.
Because each read is exactly 4 lines, number of reads = lines / 4: echo $(( $(zcat reads.fastq.gz | wc -l) / 4 )).
Quality-control tools such as FastQC summarize quality scores across a whole file.

title: Common Data Formats & Public Repositories
text:
Compressed files (.gz) and streaming
Sequencing and other large text files are almost always stored gzip-compressed (.gz), often 3-5x smaller. You rarely need to decompress them to disk; instead stream them through a pipe:
zcat reads.fastq.gz | head -n 8          # first two reads
zcat reads.fastq.gz | wc -l              # total lines
zcat genome.fa.gz | grep -c '>'          # number of sequences
zless annotation.gtf.gz                  # page through interactively

gzip results.tsv                         # compress (creates results.tsv.gz, removes original)
gunzip results.tsv.gz                    # decompress
gzip -k results.tsv                      # -k keeps the original
On macOS, the built-in zcat expects .Z files; use gzcat file.gz or zcat < file.gz instead. Some genomics files use bgzip (block gzip), which is still readable with zcat but also allows indexed random access (e.g., with tabix or samtools). Other archive types you will see: .zip (unzip), .tar.gz/.tgz (tar -xzf file.tar.gz), and .bz2 (bzcat).

title: Common Data Formats & Public Repositories
text:
Alignments: SAM and BAM
When reads are aligned to a reference genome, the result is stored as SAM (Sequence Alignment/Map; tab-delimited text with a @ header section and one line per alignment) or its compressed binary equivalent BAM (.bam, with an index .bai). Use samtools [@li2009samtools; @danecek2021twelve] to work with them (its sibling bcftools does the same for VCF):
samtools view -H sample.bam | head       # header lines
samtools view sample.bam | head -n 3     # first 3 alignments as SAM text
samtools flagstat sample.bam             # summary: how many reads mapped

title: Common Data Formats & Public Repositories
text:
Genomic annotation and interval formats
All are tab-delimited text, one feature per line; chromosome names must match the reference genome you use.

GFF3 / GTF (.gff3, .gtf): nine columns describing genes, transcripts, exons, and CDS features, 1-based coordinates. Reference annotation sets such as GENCODE [@frankish2021gencode] and Ensembl are distributed in this form.
chr17  HAVANA  gene  7661779  7687538  .  -  .  gene_id "ENSG00000141510"; gene_name "TP53";
BED (.bed): at minimum chromosome, start, end; used for regions, peaks, and targets. 0-based, half-open coordinates (start is counted from 0 and the end position is excluded).
chr17  7661778  7687538  TP53  0  -
VCF (.vcf, .vcf.gz): genetic variants (SNPs, indels) relative to a reference, with ## metadata lines, a #CHROM header, and optional per-sample genotype columns.
#CHROM  POS      ID         REF  ALT  QUAL  FILTER  INFO
chr17   7675088  rs28934578 C    T    60    PASS    DP=42

title: Common Data Formats & Public Repositories
text:
Hierarchical binary data: HDF5, .h5, and .h5ad
HDF5 (Hierarchical Data Format 5; .h5, .hdf5) stores many large numerical arrays and their metadata inside a single binary file organized like a file system (groups and datasets). It supports compression and lets programs read just the slice they need without loading the whole file, so it is common for microscopy and imaging data, simulation output, instrument data, and large matrices. .h5ad is the HDF5-based file format for Python’s AnnData package, widely used for large annotated matrices (e.g., samples/cells by genes).

Inspect from the shell with h5ls -r file.h5 (from the HDF5 tools).
Read in Python with h5py (or anndata.read_h5ad() for .h5ad); in R with the Bioconductor rhdf5 package.

title: Common Data Formats & Public Repositories
section: R objects: .rds and .RData vs plain text
text:
R objects: .rds and .RData vs plain text

saveRDS(obj, "file.rds") / readRDS("file.rds") saves and restores one R object exactly (including factor levels, attributes, and complex objects such as model fits).
save(a, b, file = "file.RData") / load("file.RData") stores several objects and restores them under their original names (which can silently overwrite objects in your session).

Both are convenient for work in progress and for passing results between steps of your own pipeline, but they are not good archival or sharing formats: they are readable only by R, can break across major package versions, and cannot be diffed in Git. For anything you will share, publish, or keep long-term, also write a plain-text version (readr::write_csv()) and keep the code that regenerates the R object. Avoid saving your whole workspace to .RData at exit (RStudio: Tools → Global Options → General, set “Save workspace” to Never). See ?@sec-r-programming and ?@sec-appendix-r.

title: Common Data Formats & Public Repositories
text:
Structured text: JSON and YAML
Both represent nested key-value data in plain text and are common for configuration files, metadata, pipeline parameters, and web APIs.
JSON (.json) uses braces, brackets, and quoted keys:
{
  "experiment": "hydrogel_swelling",
  "temperature_C": 37,
  "replicates": [1, 2, 3],
  "instrument": {"name": "rheometer", "geometry": "parallel plate"}
}
YAML (.yml, .yaml) expresses the same structure with indentation, and is what Quarto uses for document headers and _quarto.yml project files (?@sec-quarto-documents):
experiment: hydrogel_swelling
temperature_C: 37
replicates: [1, 2, 3]
instrument:
  name: rheometer
  geometry: parallel plate
YAML is whitespace-sensitive: use spaces (never tabs) and keep indentation consistent. Read JSON with jsonlite in R or the json module in Python; jq is a handy command-line JSON tool. Many pipelines write a params.json or config.yaml describing a run; archive it with your outputs as the “lab notebook entry” for your computational analysis.

title: Common Data Formats & Public Repositories
section: NCBI (US National Center for Biotechnology Information)
text:
NCBI (US National Center for Biotechnology Information)

GEO (Gene Expression Omnibus): processed functional-genomics data (expression tables, count matrices, sample metadata) from microarray and sequencing studies [@barrett2013geo]. Series have GSE###### accessions, and each sample has a GSM###### record. When a paper says “data are available at GEO under GSE#####”, open the series page, check the sample list, and scroll to Supplementary file to download. In R, the Bioconductor GEOquery package (getGEO(), getGEOSuppFiles()) retrieves these directly.
SRA (Sequence Read Archive) [@leinonen2011sra]: raw sequencing reads (FASTQ/BAM). Accessions: SRR (run), SRX (experiment), SRP (study). Use it when you need to re-process data from scratch. Files are big (often several to tens of GB per sample), so plan storage (e.g., Talapas project or scratch space, Lecture 10) before downloading.
GenBank / RefSeq: GenBank is the archive of all submitted nucleotide sequences; RefSeq is NCBI’s curated, non-redundant set of reference sequences (accessions like NM_ for mRNA, NP_ for protein, NC_ for chromosomes). Download records as FASTA from the page’s Send to menu or with NCBI’s datasets command-line tool.
BioProject / BioSample: the umbrella records that tie a study (PRJNA…) and its biological samples (SAMN…) to the associated GEO, SRA, and GenBank entries.







Tip



Getting raw reads. Two practical routes:

sra-tools on the command line: prefetch SRR12345678 then fasterq-dump --split-files SRR12345678 (gives paired _1.fastq and _2.fastq). On Talapas, look for it with module spider sra-tools, or install it with conda/Bioconda.
SRA Explorer: paste in an accession and it returns ready-to-use wget/curl download commands, usually pointing at the ENA mirror.

title: Common Data Formats & Public Repositories
text:
EBI / ENA (Europe)
The European Bioinformatics Institute runs the European counterparts: the European Nucleotide Archive (ENA) mirrors SRA and GenBank (the same SRR… accessions work) and often provides direct FTP/HTTPS links to FASTQ files that you can wget without sra-tools. BioStudies / ArrayExpress is the European counterpart to GEO, and UniProt is the central resource for protein sequences and functional annotation.

title: Common Data Formats & Public Repositories
section: Reference genomes and annotations: UCSC and Ensembl
text:
Reference genomes and annotations: UCSC and Ensembl

UCSC Genome Browser: interactive browser for genomes and annotation tracks, plus bulk downloads of genome FASTA, annotation files, and the Table Browser for exporting regions as BED/GTF. Assemblies are named like hg38 (human) or mm39 (mouse).
Ensembl: genome browser and annotation database with stable gene IDs (ENSG…) and a public FTP site for genome FASTA and GTF/GFF3 files for hundreds of vertebrate species (plus Ensembl Genomes for plants, fungi, bacteria, and invertebrates).

Always record which assembly and annotation release you used (e.g., GRCh38, Ensembl release number), because coordinates and gene models change between versions. Note also that UCSC names chromosomes chr1 while Ensembl uses 1.

title: Common Data Formats & Public Repositories
text:
Protein structures: Protein Data Bank
The RCSB Protein Data Bank (PDB) archives experimentally determined 3D structures of proteins, nucleic acids, and complexes, each with a four-character ID (e.g., 1TUP). Download coordinates as .pdb or the newer .cif (mmCIF) text formats; view them in the browser, or in tools like PyMOL or ChimeraX. The AlphaFold Protein Structure Database provides predicted structures for most known proteins.

title: Common Data Formats & Public Repositories
text:
General-purpose repositories: Zenodo, Figshare, Dryad
For data that do not fit a specialized repository (imaging, mechanical testing, simulation output, code, and supplementary tables), general-purpose repositories assign each deposit a permanent DOI so it can be cited:

Zenodo (run by CERN): free; integrates with GitHub to archive a tagged release of a code repository with a DOI.
Figshare: used by many journals for supplementary data.
Dryad: curated repository for data underlying publications, common in ecology, evolution, and biology.

title: Common Data Formats & Public Repositories
text:
FAIR Data and Public Repositories
Everything above is about finding and reading other people’s data. Sooner or later you will be on the other side: a journal, a funder (the NIH Data Management and Sharing Policy applies to all NIH-funded work since 2023), or a collaborator will ask for yours. Done well, sharing produces citations (reanalysis papers cite their input datasets), a one-line answer to “can I see your raw data?”, and compliance that passes review. Done poorly, the dataset sits on a lab drive until it is unreadable. The cost of doing it well is paid up front, during the project; the payoff lasts the lifetime of the data.

The FAIR Principles
Wilkinson et al. [@wilkinson2016fair] proposed four principles for data that people and machines can reuse (Table 5).



Table 5: The four FAIR principles [@wilkinson2016fair] and their practical consequences










Principle
One-line definition
What it means for you




Findable
Data and metadata have a persistent identifier and are indexed in a searchable registry
Get an accession (GEO, SRA, BioProject) or a DOI (Zenodo, Dryad); a lab website is not enough


Accessible
Anyone (or anyone authorized) can retrieve the data by that identifier through an open, standard protocol
HTTPS/FTP download; controlled access is fine for sensitive human data, as long as the procedure is open


Interoperable
Data use shared formats and controlled vocabularies so datasets combine cleanly
CSV/FASTA/FASTQ rather than proprietary formats; standard units; ontology terms rather than free text


Reusable
Provenance, a clear license, and enough metadata for someone else to reanalyze
README, data dictionary, software versions, license file






FAIR is not the same as open: patient genomes in a controlled-access archive can satisfy all four criteria. The principle most datasets fail is I: “B cells” in a free-text column is a different string from “B-cell”, “Bcell”, and “B_cell” to a computer, so every downstream integration needs a human to reconcile terms. The most common omission is F: data deposited without a stable identifier, or not indexed where searchers look.


Where Data Go: The NCBI Hierarchy
For sequencing-based studies the canonical archive is NCBI (mirrored by EBI/ENA), and its records nest (Table 6). The same structure applies to bulk RNA-seq, ChIP-seq, genome resequencing, microbiome amplicons, and any other sequencing assay.



Table 6: The NCBI record hierarchy for sequencing data











Record
Accession
What it holds
How many




BioProject
PRJNA######
The study as a whole: title, abstract, grant, publication
One per paper


BioSample
SAMN########
One biological sample: organism, tissue, donor or strain, treatment, collection date
One per sample


SRA run
SRR#######
The raw reads (FASTQ or BAM) from one sequencing run, linked to its BioSample [@leinonen2011sra]
One or more per sample


GEO series / sample
GSE###### / GSM######
Processed expression data: count matrices, normalized tables, and the sample metadata; GEO creates the SRA and BioSample records for you when you submit expression data [@barrett2013geo]
One series per study, one GSM per sample






The submission order follows the hierarchy: create the BioProject, register BioSamples, upload raw reads to SRA (each run linked to its SAMN), then, for expression studies, submit processed data and metadata to GEO, which links back to the BioProject and SRA runs. Cite every accession in the paper’s Data Availability statement. Non-sequencing data (imaging, mechanical testing, simulations, code) go to a general-purpose repository with a DOI (Zenodo, Figshare, Dryad, above).


The Canonical Sample Sheet
Most of the work of sharing is metadata, and the discipline that makes it painless is a single canonical sample sheet, started at experimental design time and kept under version control alongside your code. “Sample 1, Sample 2, Sample 3” is not metadata; at minimum the sheet answers who or what the sample came from, what tissue or material, what condition or treatment, what protocol, who processed it, when, on what instrument, with what software version. Its rules:

One row per sample, one column per variable (this is ?@sec-tidy-data applied to your experiment).
A stable, unique sample_id that never changes and appears in every file name, every FASTQ header you can control, and every downstream table. NCBI links BioSample, SRA, and GEO records by this ID, and the match is case-sensitive and literal: donor1_CTRL and Donor1_CTRL will not link. Manual retyping of sample names across three submission spreadsheets is the single most common cause of broken submissions.
Controlled vocabularies, not free text, for anything you will filter or join on: fixed spellings for conditions (control/treated, not ctrl, Control, CTRL), standard units in the column name (stiffness_kPa), ISO dates (2026-03-14), and, where an ontology exists, its term ID (Uberon for tissues, NCBI Taxonomy for organisms, Cell Ontology for cell types, EFO for assays; look them up at the Ontology Lookup Service).
Metadata columns for every batch effect you can record: extraction date, library prep kit and lot, sequencing run, operator. You cannot correct for a batch you did not write down.

sample_id      donor_id  tissue_ontology  condition  replicate  extraction_date  library_kit     run_id
donor1_ctrl    D001      UBERON:0000178   control    1          2026-02-03       TruSeq_v2_lot7  RUN_0412
donor1_treat   D001      UBERON:0000178   treated    1          2026-02-03       TruSeq_v2_lot7  RUN_0412
donor2_ctrl    D002      UBERON:0000178   control    2          2026-02-10       TruSeq_v2_lot7  RUN_0413
At submission time every upload template (BioSample, SRA, GEO) is derived programmatically from this one sheet with a few lines of dplyr::transmute() or pandas, so that names, dates, and IDs appear in exactly one place and inconsistencies are fixed there and propagate everywhere.


Plan Sharing at Design Time
The biggest mistake is thinking about deposition only when the manuscript is in revision. By then the sample metadata is scattered across several lab notebooks, the ontology terms have to be reconstructed from memory, and the person who ran the samples has graduated. Instead, at design time:

Start the canonical sample sheet with every column deposition will need, and update it as samples arrive.
Decide which repositories the data will go to and check their required metadata fields now, not later.
Keep raw data read-only in a clearly named directory (?@sec-talapas-storage) and never edit it in place.
Record software versions and parameters for every processing step in the analysis code or a config.yaml (above).



Checksums, README, Data Dictionary, License
Four small files travel with a well-shared dataset.
Checksums prove that a file arrived intact. Compute one when you create or download a file and compare it after every transfer (repositories publish theirs; SRA and ENA list MD5 sums per file):
md5sum sample_R1.fastq.gz                    # prints a 32-character fingerprint
md5sum *.fastq.gz > checksums.md5             # record fingerprints for a directory
md5sum -c checksums.md5                       # later, or on another machine: verify
On macOS use md5 file or shasum -a 256 file. A single changed byte, a truncated download, or a job killed mid-write (see ?@sec-right-sizing) produces a different checksum, which is far easier to notice than a subtly corrupt file.
A README (plain text or Markdown, at the top of the dataset) says what the data are, who generated them, when, with what instrument and protocol, how the files are organized, and how to cite them. A data dictionary describes every column of every table: name, meaning, type, units, allowed values, and how missing values are coded. Together they are what turns a directory of files into something a stranger can use.
A license states what others may do with the data; without one, reuse is legally ambiguous even if the files are public. Common choices are CC0 (public domain, the default at many repositories and the simplest for data) and CC BY (reuse with attribution); code is usually released under a software license such as MIT or GPL instead. Human-subject data may need a data-use agreement rather than an open license; your IRB and repository will say which.






Tip



A minimal FAIR checklist for any dataset. A persistent identifier (accession or DOI); open, plain-text formats where possible; a canonical sample sheet with stable IDs and controlled vocabularies; a README and data dictionary; recorded software versions; checksums; and a license. See also the GO FAIR initiative.
