A programming language that is interpreted at runtime rather than compiled ahead of time, making it fast to write and iterate. Bash, R, and Python are all scripting languages. Learn more →

seff

A SLURM utility (installed on most clusters, including Talapas) that prints a friendly summary of a completed job’s CPU efficiency, memory efficiency, and wall time: seff <jobid>. The quickest way to right-size future submissions. Learn more →

Sequence Read Archive (SRA)

NCBI’s repository for raw sequencing reads (FASTQ/BAM), linked to GEO series through BioProject and BioSample accessions. Downloaded with sra-tools (prefetch + fasterq-dump) or from the European mirror (ENA). See Appendix G. Learn more →

Shell

A command interpreter that accepts text commands, passes them to the operating system, and returns output as text. Bash and zsh (the default on modern macOS) are the most common shells for scientific computing. The shell is also a scripting language: commands saved in a .sh file can be re-run non-interactively. Learn more →

Shell script

A text file of shell commands, usually starting with a shebang line (e.g., #!/bin/bash), that can be executed as a program. Shell scripts automate repetitive tasks, chain analysis steps into pipelines, and serve as the job scripts submitted to SLURM. Covered in Lecture 06 and Appendix B. Learn more →

SLURM

The Simple Linux Utility for Resource Management, the scheduler used on Talapas and most academic HPC clusters. It accepts job submissions (sbatch, srun), places jobs on appropriate compute nodes, enforces resource limits (--mem, --time), and provides accounting (sacct, seff). Covered in Lecture 10. Learn more →

SLURM commands (quick list)

sbatch (submit a batch script), srun (run a command or interactive shell), squeue -u $USER (list your jobs), scancel <id> (cancel), sinfo (partition status), sacct and seff (usage after a job ends). Each has its own entry in this glossary. Learn more →

Snakemake

A Python-based workflow manager that describes a pipeline as rules with input: and output: files, automatically re-running only rules whose inputs have changed and running independent rules in parallel. A natural upgrade from shell scripts for pipelines that process many samples or must restart after partial failures. Learn more →

Sparse matrix

A storage format for matrices that are mostly zeros. Instead of keeping every zero, a sparse matrix saves only the non-zero values and their positions, saving memory and speeding up calculations (e.g., the R Matrix package, Python scipy.sparse). Learn more →

squeue

The SLURM command to list queued and running jobs. squeue -u $USER shows your jobs with state codes (PD pending, R running, CG completing) and a Reason column explaining why pending jobs have not started. Finished jobs disappear from squeue; use seff or sacct afterward. Learn more →

srun

The SLURM command to launch a job step or start an interactive session on a compute node; srun --pty bash (with --account, --partition, --mem, and --time flags) requests an interactive shell. Learn more →

SSD (Solid-State Drive)

A storage device that uses flash memory with no moving parts, offering much lower access latency (~0.1 ms) and higher throughput than an HDD. Keeping large input files on an SSD noticeably speeds up loading them. Learn more →

SSH (Secure Shell)

A cryptographic network protocol for authenticated, encrypted remote login. On Talapas, ssh <duckid>@login.talapas.uoregon.edu opens a shell on a login node, and VS Code Remote-SSH uses the same protocol to connect the editor to the cluster. Learn more →

SSH key

A cryptographic key pair (public + private) that authenticates SSH connections without typing a password. Generate one with ssh-keygen -t ed25519; the public key (~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub) is copied to a server or added to GitHub, while the private key never leaves your computer. Learn more →

SSH tunneling

Forwarding a network port from a remote server through an encrypted SSH connection to your local machine (e.g., ssh -L 8888:localhost:8888 ...), commonly used to reach a Jupyter or RStudio server running on a compute node from a local web browser. Learn more →

Staging area

In Git, the intermediate zone (also called the index) where changes are placed with git add before being recorded in a commit. It lets you package related changes into logically coherent commits rather than committing every modified file at once. Learn more →

stdin / stdout / stderr

The three standard streams every Unix process inherits: stdin (stream 0) is input (keyboard or a redirected file with <); stdout (stream 1) is normal output (terminal, or a file with >); stderr (stream 2) carries error and status messages (redirected separately with 2>). Pipes connect stdout of one command to stdin of the next. Learn more →

Symbolic link

A filesystem entry that points to another file or directory rather than containing data itself, like a desktop shortcut. Created with ln -s target linkname; on clusters, symlinks give projects easy access to shared reference data without duplicating large files. Learn more →

Syntax highlighting

The automatic coloring of different parts of source code (keywords, strings, comments, function names) in a code editor. RStudio, Positron, and VS Code highlight R, Python, Bash, and Quarto documents, making code easier to read and errors easier to spot. Learn more →

title: Glossary
text:
tabix

A tool from the htslib suite that indexes a coordinate-sorted, BGZF-compressed tab-delimited file (VCF, BED, GFF) so you can quickly pull out the lines for a genomic region without scanning the whole file. Learn more →

Tag

In Git, a named, fixed reference to a specific commit, most often used to mark releases (e.g., v1.0). Unlike branches, tags do not move as new commits are added, making them good for citing the exact version of code used in a paper. Learn more →

Talapas

The University of Oregon’s HPC cluster, managed by RACS. It provides thousands of CPU cores, GPUs, and large shared storage, and is accessed via SSH or Open OnDemand using your Duck ID and Duo two-step login. Covered in ?@sec-hpc-talapas. Learn more →

Teams / SharePoint

Microsoft’s group collaboration tools within Microsoft 365. Teams provides chat, meetings, and shared files for a lab or class; the files behind a Team live in SharePoint, storage owned by the group rather than by any one person, which makes it the right home for lab documents that must outlast individual members. Approved at UO for amber and, like OneDrive, HIPAA data. See ?@sec-computing-at-uo. Learn more →

Terminal

An application that provides a text window in which you interact with a shell. On macOS the built-in app is Terminal; on Windows, WSL provides an Ubuntu terminal; RStudio, Positron, and VS Code all have a built-in terminal. “Terminal” and “command line” are often used interchangeably. Learn more →

Text editor

A program for creating and editing plain-text files without the hidden formatting of word processors. Simple editors (nano, vim) run in a terminal; feature-rich editors (VS Code, Positron, RStudio) add syntax highlighting, autocompletion, and Git integration. R scripts, shell scripts, and .qmd files are all plain text. Learn more →

tibble

An enhanced data frame from the tibble package (part of the tidyverse) that prints more concisely, never converts strings to factors, and gives clearer error messages. read_csv() returns a tibble; as_tibble() converts an existing data frame. Learn more →

tidyverse

A collection of R packages (including dplyr, ggplot2, tidyr, readr, purrr, and tibble) built around a consistent, pipe-friendly grammar for data import, tidying, transformation, and visualization. Loaded with library(tidyverse). Learn more →

TinyTeX

A lightweight, easy-to-maintain LaTeX distribution designed for R Markdown and Quarto users. Install it with quarto install tinytex so Quarto can render PDF documents; missing LaTeX packages are installed automatically as needed. Learn more →

TSV

Tab-Separated Values, a plain-text format like CSV but using tab characters as delimiters. Common for genomics tables and annotation files because text fields may themselves contain commas. Read with read_tsv() in the tidyverse or pandas.read_csv(sep="\t") in Python. Learn more →

title: Glossary
text:
VCF (Variant Call Format)

A tab-delimited format for genomic variant calls (SNVs, indels, structural variants) relative to a reference, with a ## metadata header, mandatory columns (CHROM, POS, ID, REF, ALT, QUAL, FILTER, INFO), and optional per-sample genotype columns. BCF is its binary equivalent. Learn more →

Vector

R’s fundamental data structure: an ordered sequence of values that are all the same type (numeric, character, logical). Most R operations are vectorized, applying element-wise to every value at once. Learn more →

Vectorization

The property of R (and NumPy in Python) whereby operations automatically apply element-wise to every element of a vector or column, with no explicit loop. For example, force_N > 4 tests every element of force_N in one expression. Vectorized code is shorter and usually much faster than loops. Learn more →

Version control

The practice of systematically tracking changes to files over time so that earlier states can be recovered, alternative versions developed in parallel branches, and contributions from collaborators merged. Git is the dominant version-control system in science and engineering. Learn more →

Virtual environment

An isolated set of installed packages for one project, so that different projects can use different package versions without interfering. In Python, python3 -m venv .venv creates one and source .venv/bin/activate turns it on; conda and uv are alternatives, and renv plays the same role in R. Standard practice on Talapas. See ?@sec-toolkit. Learn more →

Virtual machine (VM)

A software emulation of an entire computer (hardware, operating system, and installed programs) that runs inside a host computer. VMs can run Linux on a Windows or Mac laptop; WSL uses a lightweight VM, and containers are an even lighter-weight alternative. Learn more →

VPN (Virtual Private Network)

An encrypted connection between your computer and an organization’s network that makes your traffic appear to come from inside that network. Some university resources may require a VPN connection when you work off campus; see ?@sec-computing-at-uo and the UO IT documentation for current guidance; for Talapas the VPN is recommended but not required. Learn more →

VS Code (Visual Studio Code)

A free, cross-platform code editor and IDE from Microsoft, built on the open-source Code OSS project, that supports R, Python, Bash, and Quarto through extensions. It includes syntax highlighting, autocompletion, Git integration, an integrated terminal, and Remote-SSH for working on Talapas. See Appendix A. Learn more →

title: Glossary
text:
Wall-clock time vs CPU time

Wall-clock time is elapsed real time, which is what --time limits and what seff reports as “Job Wall-clock time.” CPU time is roughly wall-clock time × cores used and measures total processor work: a 1-hour job on 8 cores consumes about 8 CPU-hours but 1 hour of walltime. Learn more →

Walltime / time limit

The maximum elapsed time a SLURM job may run, set with --time=HH:MM:SS (or D-HH:MM:SS). When the limit is reached SLURM terminates the job with state TIMEOUT, so leave a reasonable margin. Learn more →

wget / curl

Command-line tools for downloading files from URLs. wget URL saves the file to the current directory; curl -L -o filename URL saves to a named file. Both pull reference genomes, datasets, and software directly onto a server or cluster without a browser. Learn more →

Wildcard / globbing

Patterns that the shell expands into matching filenames before passing them to a command: * matches any string, ? matches one character, and [abc] matches one character from the set. For example, ls *.csv lists all CSV files. “Globbing” is the name for this expansion. Learn more →

Workflow manager

A tool (Snakemake, Nextflow) that represents a computational pipeline as a dependency graph (DAG) of inputs and outputs, tracking which steps are complete, skipping finished stages, and rerunning only affected steps when inputs change. A more robust alternative to hand-written shell scripts for multi-sample pipelines. Learn more →

Working directory

The directory a process is currently “standing in,” used as the starting point for relative paths. In the shell, pwd prints it and cd changes it; in R, getwd() and setwd(); in Python, os.getcwd(). Learn more →

WSL (Windows Subsystem for Linux)

A Windows feature that runs a real Linux environment (Ubuntu by default) directly on Windows, giving you a Bash shell and Linux tools without a separate computer or dual-boot. Install it with wsl --install in an administrator PowerShell window; your Windows files appear under /mnt/c/Users/<name>. See Appendix A. Learn more →

title: Glossary
text:
YAML header

The block of configuration at the top of a Quarto .qmd file, delimited by --- lines and written in YAML (a recursive acronym for “YAML Ain’t Markup Language”). It sets the document title, author, output format, and execution options (e.g., eval: false). YAML is also used for many configuration files, including Quarto’s _quarto.yml. Learn more →

title: Glossary
text:
Zotero

A free, open-source reference manager. Its browser connector saves a paper’s citation and PDF with one click, group libraries share a reading list with a lab, and it inserts citations and bibliographies into Word and Quarto documents. See ?@sec-computing-at-uo. Learn more →



A few general definitions (e.g., Algorithm, Benchmark, Pipeline, Sparse matrix) are adapted, with modifications, from the Single-cell best practices glossary (Heumos et al.). All other entries were written for this course.

title: Files, Pipes, and Redirection
text:
NoteLearning Objectives



After completing this chapter, you will be able to:

Explain the Unix philosophy and how it shapes command-line tools
Read files efficiently using cat, less, head, and tail
Use input and output redirection to work with files
Chain commands together using pipes
Apply these tools to process genomic data files



In the previous chapter (?@sec-unix-fundamentals), you learned to navigate the filesystem and manipulate files—creating, copying, moving, and deleting them. But files contain data, and data science is ultimately about extracting meaning from data. In this chapter, we explore how Unix tools let you examine, transform, and combine data with remarkable elegance.
The secret to Unix’s power lies in its philosophy of small, focused tools that work together through pipes and redirection. Instead of one massive program that tries to do everything, Unix provides dozens of simple tools that you can combine in endless ways. Learning to think in terms of pipelines—data flowing from one tool to the next—will transform how you approach computational problems.


Unix tools are designed around a simple but powerful philosophy [@kernighan1984unix]:

Write programs that do one thing and do it well. Write programs to work together. Write programs to handle text streams, because that is a universal interface.

This philosophy has profound implications for how you work:

Small, focused tools: Each command does one specific task excellently
Composition: Complex operations are built by combining simple tools
Text as interface: Programs communicate through text, making them compatible

Understanding this philosophy transforms how you approach computational problems. Instead of seeking one program that does everything, you learn to construct pipelines from simple components.



Every Unix program has three standard communication channels, called streams. Understanding these streams is essential to understanding how Unix tools communicate with each other and with you.
         ┌──────────────┐
stdin ───>│              │───> stdout
    (0)   │   Program    │      (1)
          │              │───> stderr
          └──────────────┘      (2)

Standard Input (stdin)

Where programs read input. By default, this is your keyboard—when a program waits for input, it’s reading from stdin. File descriptor 0.

Standard Output (stdout)

Where programs write normal output. By default, this appears on your terminal screen. When you run ls, the file listing goes to stdout. File descriptor 1.

Standard Error (stderr)

Where programs write error messages. This also appears on your terminal by default, but it’s a separate channel from stdout. This separation lets you capture errors separately from normal output. File descriptor 2.


The magic of Unix is that these streams can be redirected—connected to files instead of the keyboard or screen, or piped directly into other programs. This is what makes it possible to build powerful pipelines where data flows through a series of transformations.



Before you can process data, you need to see what’s in your files. In a graphical environment, you might double-click a file to open it in an application. In Unix, we have several tools for examining file contents, each suited to different situations.


Choosing the right viewing tool depends on your goal and the file’s size. Table 1 summarizes when to use each:



Table 1: File reading commands and their uses





Command
Best For




cat
Small files, concatenating files


less
Large files, browsing, searching


head
First few lines of a file


tail
Last few lines, monitoring logs


wc
Counting lines, words, characters









The cat command (short for “concatenate”) is the simplest way to view a file—it dumps the entire contents to stdout. The name reflects its original purpose: concatenating (joining) multiple files together.
# Display a file
$ cat data.txt

# Display multiple files (concatenated together)
$ cat header.txt data.txt footer.txt

# Number the output lines
$ cat -n data.txt

# Show non-printing characters (useful for debugging whitespace issues)
$ cat -A data.txt
The cat command is similar to print() in R—it simply outputs what you give it. This makes it useful for small files and for combining files, but it’s not appropriate for large files.






Warning



Never use cat on large files! It will flood your terminal with text, and there’s no way to stop it except Ctrl+C. For genomic data files (which can be gigabytes), always use head to peek at the beginning, less to browse interactively, or process through pipes.





For large files, less is the tool of choice. It’s a pager—a program that displays content one screen at a time, letting you scroll forward and backward, search for patterns, and navigate through gigabytes of data without loading it all into memory.
$ less huge_file.txt
If you’re wondering about the name: the original pager was called more (as in “show me more of this file”). When a better version was created, someone named it less because “less is more.”
Key navigation commands in less are listed in Table 2:



Table 2: Navigation keys in less





Key
Action




Space, f
Forward one page


b
Back one page


g
Go to beginning


G
Go to end


/pattern
Search forward


?pattern
Search backward


n
Next search match


N
Previous search match


q
Quit









# First 10 lines (default)
$ head data.csv

# First 20 lines
$ head -n 20 data.csv

# All but the last 5 lines
$ head -n -5 data.csv

# Last 10 lines (default)
$ tail data.csv

# Last 50 lines
$ tail -n 50 data.csv

# Everything after line 100
$ tail -n +100 data.csv
A special use of tail is monitoring files that are being written:
# Follow a file as it grows (Ctrl+C to stop)
$ tail -f analysis.log
This is invaluable for watching job progress on computing clusters.




Redirection connects a program’s output to a file instead of the terminal.


# Save command output to a file
$ ls -l > file_list.txt

# Save date to a file
$ date > timestamp.txt

# Redirect output from any command
$ echo "Hello, World!" > greeting.txt






Caution



The > operator overwrites existing files without warning! Double-check your filenames before running commands with >.





# Add to an existing file
$ echo "New line" >> notes.txt

# Append today's entries to a log
$ date >> daily_log.txt
$ echo "Analysis completed" >> daily_log.txt



Sometimes you want to separate normal output from error messages:
# Send errors to a file, output to screen
$ ls /nonexistent 2> errors.txt

# Save output and errors to different files
$ command > output.txt 2> errors.txt

# Discard errors (send to /dev/null)
$ command 2> /dev/null

# Combine stdout and stderr to one file
$ command &> all_output.txt




Input redirection feeds file contents to a program’s stdin:
# Count lines in a file (two equivalent ways)
$ wc -l < data.txt
$ wc -l data.txt

# Sort input from a file
$ sort < names.txt
While many commands can read files directly as arguments, input redirection is essential for programs that only read from stdin.



Pipes (|) are the secret weapon of Unix and one of its most elegant innovations. A pipe connects the stdout of one command directly to the stdin of the next, allowing you to chain tools together into a processing pipeline:
command1 | command2 | command3
Data flows through the pipeline like water through physical pipes, transformed at each step. The output of command1 becomes the input to command2, whose output becomes the input to command3. No intermediate files are created—the data exists only in memory as it flows between programs.
This approach, combined with the Unix philosophy of small focused tools, means you can construct sophisticated data processing workflows by combining simple commands. Each command does one thing well, and the pipe connects them into something greater than the sum of its parts.






Tip



The pipe symbol | is typically located above the backslash \ on US keyboards (Shift + backslash). It may be in different locations on international keyboards.


If you’re familiar with R’s tidyverse, the Unix pipe | works similarly to R’s pipe operators (%>% or |>, introduced in ?@sec-tidy-data). In R, you might write:
data %>% filter(year > 2000) %>% summarize(mean = mean(value))
The Unix equivalent would chain commands the same way:
cat data.txt | grep "2000" | awk '{sum += $2} END {print sum/NR}'
Both pass output from one operation to the next, building complex transformations from simple steps.


Here are some basic examples to illustrate how pipes work:
# Count files in a directory
$ ls | wc -l

# Sort and remove duplicates
$ cat names.txt | sort | uniq

# Find CSV files in a listing
$ ls -l | grep "\.csv"

# Page through help output (useful for long manual pages)
$ man ls | less
$ ls --help | less
The last example is particularly practical: help pages can be long, and piping them to less lets you scroll through at your own pace.



Start simple and build up:
# Step 1: Look at raw data
$ cat data.csv | head

# Step 2: Extract a column (field 2, comma-delimited)
$ cat data.csv | cut -d',' -f2 | head

# Step 3: Remove header, sort
$ cat data.csv | cut -d',' -f2 | tail -n +2 | sort

# Step 4: Count unique values
$ cat data.csv | cut -d',' -f2 | tail -n +2 | sort | uniq -c

# Step 5: Sort by frequency
$ cat data.csv | cut -d',' -f2 | tail -n +2 | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn






TipPipeline Development Strategy




Start with head to see sample data
Add one command at a time
Verify output at each step
Build up to the complete pipeline
Save complex pipelines in scripts (?@sec-shell-scripting)






Sometimes you want to save intermediate results while continuing the pipeline. The tee command splits output:
# Save to file AND continue pipeline
$ cat data.txt | sort | tee sorted.txt | uniq
This saves the sorted data to sorted.txt while simultaneously passing it to uniq.




Several commands are designed to work in pipelines:


# Alphabetical sort
$ sort names.txt

# Numeric sort
$ sort -n numbers.txt

# Reverse sort
$ sort -r data.txt

# Sort by specific column (field 3, tab-delimited)
$ sort -t$'\t' -k3 data.tsv

# Sort numerically by field 2
$ sort -t',' -k2 -n data.csv



# Remove adjacent duplicates (requires sorted input!)
$ sort names.txt | uniq

# Count occurrences
$ sort names.txt | uniq -c

# Show only duplicated lines
$ sort names.txt | uniq -d

# Show only unique lines
$ sort names.txt | uniq -u



# Extract column 2 (tab-delimited default)
$ cut -f2 data.tsv

# Extract columns 1 and 3
$ cut -f1,3 data.tsv

# Comma-delimited
$ cut -d',' -f2 data.csv

# Character positions 1-10
$ cut -c1-10 data.txt



# Convert lowercase to uppercase
$ echo "hello" | tr 'a-z' 'A-Z'

# Delete characters
$ echo "hello123" | tr -d '0-9'

# Squeeze repeated characters
$ echo "hello    world" | tr -s ' '

# Replace characters
$ cat data.csv | tr ',' '\t'  # CSV to TSV



We’ll cover grep extensively in ?@sec-grep-regex, but here are basic uses:
# Find lines containing "error"
$ grep "error" log.txt

# Case-insensitive search
$ grep -i "warning" log.txt

# Invert match (lines NOT containing pattern)
$ grep -v "^#" data.txt  # Remove comment lines

# Count matches
$ grep -c "pattern" file.txt




Let’s apply these tools to real bioinformatics scenarios. Genomic data files are often massive—the human genome reference is over 3 GB. You must process them efficiently.


FASTA files store sequences with headers starting with >:
>sequence1 description
ATGCGATCGATCGATCGATCG
ATCGATCGATCGATCGATCGA
>sequence2 another description
GCTAGCTAGCTAGCTAGCTAG



# Download human genome from NCBI using wget
$ wget https://ftp.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/genomes/all/GCF/000/001/405/\
GCF_000001405.40_GRCh38.p14/GCF_000001405.40_GRCh38.p14_genomic.fna.gz

# Or using curl
$ curl -O https://example.com/genome.fa.gz



Most genomic data is compressed. Unix tools handle this seamlessly:
# View compressed file without extracting
$ zcat genome.fa.gz | head

# Search compressed file
$ zgrep ">" genome.fa.gz | wc -l

# Decompress and recompress
$ gunzip genome.fa.gz         # Creates genome.fa
$ gzip genome.fa              # Creates genome.fa.gz
$ gzip -k genome.fa           # Keep original file



# Count sequences (headers start with >)
$ grep -c "^>" sequences.fa

# List all sequence headers
$ grep "^>" sequences.fa

# Calculate total sequence length (remove headers and newlines)
$ grep -v "^>" genome.fa | tr -d '\n' | wc -c

# Count nucleotides
$ grep -v "^>" genome.fa | tr -d '\n' | fold -w1 | sort | uniq -c



Let’s calculate the GC content (percentage of G and C bases) of a genome:
# Extract sequence, convert to single line, count G and C
$ grep -v "^>" genome.fa | \
  tr -d '\n' | \
  tr -cd 'GCgc' | \
  wc -c
This pipeline:

grep -v "^>" — removes header lines
tr -d '\n' — removes newlines to get one long sequence
tr -cd 'GCgc' — deletes everything except G and C
wc -c — counts remaining characters







Note



The backslash \ at the end of a line continues the command on the next line, making complex pipelines more readable.





# Count EcoRI sites (GAATTC)
$ grep -v "^>" genome.fa | tr -d '\n' | grep -o "GAATTC" | wc -l

# Find all start codons (ATG) and their positions
$ grep -v "^>" genome.fa | tr -d '\n' | grep -b -o "ATG" | head -20



You can process data without saving intermediate files:
# Download, decompress, and analyze in one pipeline
$ curl -s https://url/to/genome.fa.gz | \
  gunzip -c | \
  grep -v "^>" | \
  tr -d '\n' | \
  wc -c
This streams data through memory, never writing to disk—essential when working with files larger than your available storage.







Filter early: Reduce data volume as early as possible in the pipeline
Test incrementally: Build and verify step by step
Use appropriate tools: less for viewing, head for sampling
Save complex pipelines: Put them in shell scripts (?@sec-shell-scripting)




# Check file exists before processing
$ test -f data.txt && grep "pattern" data.txt

# Preview destructive operations
$ ls *.tmp                    # See what will be deleted
$ rm *.tmp                    # Then delete

# Use tee to save intermediate results
$ complex_pipeline | tee checkpoint.txt | further_processing




This chapter covered the tools for reading, writing, and connecting Unix commands:

Standard streams (stdin, stdout, stderr) enable program communication
Output redirection (>, >>) saves results to files
Input redirection (<) feeds file contents to commands
Pipes (|) connect commands into powerful pipelines
Tools like sort, uniq, cut, tr, and grep transform data
Genomic data analysis leverages these tools at scale

The Unix pipe is one of the most elegant ideas in computing history. By designing programs that read from stdin and write to stdout, the creators of Unix made it possible to combine simple tools into sophisticated pipelines. You don’t need to write a custom program for every analysis—you can often assemble existing tools to do exactly what you need.
These concepts form the foundation of Unix data processing. Master them, and you can construct solutions to virtually any text-processing challenge. In the next chapter (?@sec-grep-regex), we’ll dive deeper into grep and regular expressions, giving you even more powerful pattern-matching capabilities.






Tip



For quick reference on Unix commands and pipeline tools covered in this chapter, see ?@sec-appendix-unix.





To explore pipes, redirection, and text processing further:

Data Science at the Command Line by Jeroen Janssens — A comprehensive guide to using command-line tools for data analysis
The Art of Command Line — A curated collection of tips and techniques for command-line mastery
AWK Programming Language — The GNU Awk manual for advanced text processing
sed & awk by Dale Dougherty and Arnold Robbins — A comprehensive guide to these powerful text manipulation tools

For bioinformatics-specific applications:

Bioinformatics Data Skills by Vince Buffalo [@buffalo2015bioinformatics] — An excellent resource covering Unix tools in a genomics context
NCBI FTP Guide — How to download genomic data from NCBI










TipPractice Exercises



Exercise 1: Redirection Practice

Use ls -la to list your home directory and save the output to home_contents.txt
Append the current date and time to the end of home_contents.txt
Count how many lines are in the file
Display only the last 5 lines

Exercise 2: Pipeline Construction
Create a file numbers.txt with one number per line (include some duplicates):
echo -e "5\n3\n8\n3\n1\n5\n9\n3\n7" > numbers.txt
Using pipes: 1. Sort the numbers numerically 2. Remove duplicates 3. Show only the top 3 numbers 4. Save the result to top_three.txt
Exercise 3: Text Processing
Given a CSV file with format name,score,grade, write a pipeline to: 1. Extract just the scores (column 2) 2. Sort them numerically in descending order 3. Calculate how many scores there are 4. Find the top 5 scores
Exercise 4: Genomic Data
Download a small bacterial genome and: 1. Count the number of sequences 2. Find the total sequence length 3. Count each nucleotide (A, T, G, C) 4. Search for a specific restriction enzyme site

Start simple and build up:
# Step 1: Look at raw data
$ cat data.csv | head

# Step 2: Extract a column (field 2, comma-delimited)
$ cat data.csv | cut -d',' -f2 | head

# Step 3: Remove header, sort
$ cat data.csv | cut -d',' -f2 | tail -n +2 | sort

# Step 4: Count unique values
$ cat data.csv | cut -d',' -f2 | tail -n +2 | sort | uniq -c

# Step 5: Sort by frequency
$ cat data.csv | cut -d',' -f2 | tail -n +2 | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn






TipPipeline Development Strategy




Start with head to see sample data
Add one command at a time
Verify output at each step
Build up to the complete pipeline
Save complex pipelines in scripts (?@sec-shell-scripting)






Sometimes you want to save intermediate results while continuing the pipeline. The tee command splits output:
# Save to file AND continue pipeline
$ cat data.txt | sort | tee sorted.txt | uniq
This saves the sorted data to sorted.txt while simultaneously passing it to uniq.

title: Files, Pipes, and Redirection
text:
Several commands are designed to work in pipelines:


# Alphabetical sort
$ sort names.txt

# Numeric sort
$ sort -n numbers.txt

# Reverse sort
$ sort -r data.txt

# Sort by specific column (field 3, tab-delimited)
$ sort -t$'\t' -k3 data.tsv

# Sort numerically by field 2
$ sort -t',' -k2 -n data.csv



# Remove adjacent duplicates (requires sorted input!)
$ sort names.txt | uniq

# Count occurrences
$ sort names.txt | uniq -c

# Show only duplicated lines
$ sort names.txt | uniq -d

# Show only unique lines
$ sort names.txt | uniq -u



# Extract column 2 (tab-delimited default)
$ cut -f2 data.tsv

# Extract columns 1 and 3
$ cut -f1,3 data.tsv

# Comma-delimited
$ cut -d',' -f2 data.csv

# Character positions 1-10
$ cut -c1-10 data.txt



# Convert lowercase to uppercase
$ echo "hello" | tr 'a-z' 'A-Z'

# Delete characters
$ echo "hello123" | tr -d '0-9'

# Squeeze repeated characters
$ echo "hello    world" | tr -s ' '

# Replace characters
$ cat data.csv | tr ',' '\t'  # CSV to TSV



We’ll cover grep extensively in ?@sec-grep-regex, but here are basic uses:
# Find lines containing "error"
$ grep "error" log.txt

# Case-insensitive search
$ grep -i "warning" log.txt

# Invert match (lines NOT containing pattern)
$ grep -v "^#" data.txt  # Remove comment lines

# Count matches
$ grep -c "pattern" file.txt

title: Files, Pipes, and Redirection
text:
Let’s apply these tools to real bioinformatics scenarios. Genomic data files are often massive—the human genome reference is over 3 GB. You must process them efficiently.


FASTA files store sequences with headers starting with >:
>sequence1 description
ATGCGATCGATCGATCGATCG
ATCGATCGATCGATCGATCGA
>sequence2 another description
GCTAGCTAGCTAGCTAGCTAG



# Download human genome from NCBI using wget
$ wget https://ftp.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/genomes/all/GCF/000/001/405/\
GCF_000001405.40_GRCh38.p14/GCF_000001405.40_GRCh38.p14_genomic.fna.gz

# Or using curl
$ curl -O https://example.com/genome.fa.gz



Most genomic data is compressed. Unix tools handle this seamlessly:
# View compressed file without extracting
$ zcat genome.fa.gz | head

# Search compressed file
$ zgrep ">" genome.fa.gz | wc -l

# Decompress and recompress
$ gunzip genome.fa.gz         # Creates genome.fa
$ gzip genome.fa              # Creates genome.fa.gz
$ gzip -k genome.fa           # Keep original file



# Count sequences (headers start with >)
$ grep -c "^>" sequences.fa

# List all sequence headers
$ grep "^>" sequences.fa

# Calculate total sequence length (remove headers and newlines)
$ grep -v "^>" genome.fa | tr -d '\n' | wc -c

# Count nucleotides
$ grep -v "^>" genome.fa | tr -d '\n' | fold -w1 | sort | uniq -c



Let’s calculate the GC content (percentage of G and C bases) of a genome:
# Extract sequence, convert to single line, count G and C
$ grep -v "^>" genome.fa | \
  tr -d '\n' | \
  tr -cd 'GCgc' | \
  wc -c
This pipeline:

grep -v "^>" — removes header lines
tr -d '\n' — removes newlines to get one long sequence
tr -cd 'GCgc' — deletes everything except G and C
wc -c — counts remaining characters







Note



The backslash \ at the end of a line continues the command on the next line, making complex pipelines more readable.





# Count EcoRI sites (GAATTC)
$ grep -v "^>" genome.fa | tr -d '\n' | grep -o "GAATTC" | wc -l

# Find all start codons (ATG) and their positions
$ grep -v "^>" genome.fa | tr -d '\n' | grep -b -o "ATG" | head -20



You can process data without saving intermediate files:
# Download, decompress, and analyze in one pipeline
$ curl -s https://url/to/genome.fa.gz | \
  gunzip -c | \
  grep -v "^>" | \
  tr -d '\n' | \
  wc -c
This streams data through memory, never writing to disk—essential when working with files larger than your available storage.

title: Files, Pipes, and Redirection
text:
Filter early: Reduce data volume as early as possible in the pipeline
Test incrementally: Build and verify step by step
Use appropriate tools: less for viewing, head for sampling
Save complex pipelines: Put them in shell scripts (?@sec-shell-scripting)




# Check file exists before processing
$ test -f data.txt && grep "pattern" data.txt

# Preview destructive operations
$ ls *.tmp                    # See what will be deleted
$ rm *.tmp                    # Then delete

# Use tee to save intermediate results
$ complex_pipeline | tee checkpoint.txt | further_processing

title: Files, Pipes, and Redirection
text:
This chapter covered the tools for reading, writing, and connecting Unix commands:

Standard streams (stdin, stdout, stderr) enable program communication
Output redirection (>, >>) saves results to files
Input redirection (<) feeds file contents to commands
Pipes (|) connect commands into powerful pipelines
Tools like sort, uniq, cut, tr, and grep transform data
Genomic data analysis leverages these tools at scale

The Unix pipe is one of the most elegant ideas in computing history. By designing programs that read from stdin and write to stdout, the creators of Unix made it possible to combine simple tools into sophisticated pipelines. You don’t need to write a custom program for every analysis—you can often assemble existing tools to do exactly what you need.
These concepts form the foundation of Unix data processing. Master them, and you can construct solutions to virtually any text-processing challenge. In the next chapter (?@sec-grep-regex), we’ll dive deeper into grep and regular expressions, giving you even more powerful pattern-matching capabilities.






Tip



For quick reference on Unix commands and pipeline tools covered in this chapter, see ?@sec-appendix-unix.

title: Files, Pipes, and Redirection
text:
To explore pipes, redirection, and text processing further:

Data Science at the Command Line by Jeroen Janssens — A comprehensive guide to using command-line tools for data analysis
The Art of Command Line — A curated collection of tips and techniques for command-line mastery
AWK Programming Language — The GNU Awk manual for advanced text processing
sed & awk by Dale Dougherty and Arnold Robbins — A comprehensive guide to these powerful text manipulation tools

For bioinformatics-specific applications:

Bioinformatics Data Skills by Vince Buffalo [@buffalo2015bioinformatics] — An excellent resource covering Unix tools in a genomics context
NCBI FTP Guide — How to download genomic data from NCBI

text:
TipPractice Exercises

Append the current date and time to the end of home_contents.txt
Count how many lines are in the file
Display only the last 5 lines

Exercise 2: Pipeline Construction

echo -e "5\n3\n8\n3\n1\n5\n9\n3\n7" > numbers.txt
Using pipes: 1. Sort the numbers numerically 2. Remove duplicates 3. Show only the top 3 numbers 4. Save the result to top_three.txt

Exercise 4: Genomic Data

title: Writing Functions in R
text:
NoteLearning Objectives



After completing this chapter, you will be able to:

Write your own R functions using proper syntax
Specify function arguments with default values
Return single or multiple values from functions
Use control flow (if/else, case_when) within functions
Understand lexical scoping and function environments
Apply functional programming principles with lapply and purrr
Iterate over single and multiple inputs efficiently
Choose between for loops and functional approaches





Throughout this book, we’ve used many functions: some from base R [@rproject2024] (like mean() and sum()), others from packages (like dplyr::filter() and ggplot2::ggplot()) [@wickham2019tidyverse]. But the real power of programming comes from writing your own functions. (?@sec-writing-simple-functions gave a first taste; here we go further.)
Functions allow you to avoid repetition by writing code once and using it many times. When you find yourself copying and pasting the same block of code with minor changes, that’s a sign you should write a function. This also reduces errors—if you find a bug, you fix it in one place rather than tracking down every copy. Functions improve readability by letting you give meaningful names to complex operations; calculate_gc_content(sequence) is far clearer than the five lines of code it might contain. And functions make it easy to share code with colleagues or package your solutions for the broader community.
In biosciences, you’ll often need custom functions for domain-specific tasks: calculating enzyme kinetics parameters, normalizing gene expression data, computing population genetics statistics, or processing experimental replicates according to your lab’s specific protocols.



All R functions follow the same basic syntax:
function_name = function(ARGUMENTS) {
  OPERATIONS
  return(VALUE)
}
Let’s break this down:

function_name: A descriptive name for your function
ARGUMENTS: Input values the function accepts
OPERATIONS: What the function does
return(VALUE): What the function gives back

For short functions, you can write everything on one line:
my_short_func = function(x) x^2






Tip



Give your functions short, descriptive names that indicate what they do. calculate_gc_content is better than func1 or cgc.





Let’s write a function that calculates the GC content of a DNA sequence — the proportion of guanine (G) and cytosine (C) bases. (The same function is written in Python in ?@sec-py-functions.)

gc_content = function(sequence) {
  # Convert to uppercase for consistency
  seq_upper = toupper(sequence)

  # Count G and C bases
  gc_count = str_count(seq_upper, "[GC]")

  # Calculate total length (excluding any non-ATGC characters)
  total_bases = str_count(seq_upper, "[ATGC]")

  # Return GC proportion
  gc_count / total_bases
}

Test it:

gc_content("ATGCGATCGATCG")

[1] 0.5384615

gc_content("atgcGATCgatcg")  # Works with mixed case

[1] 0.5384615

gc_content("AAAAAATTTTTT")   # Low GC content

[1] 0

gc_content("GGGGGGCCCCCC")   # High GC content

[1] 1




In the example above, R automatically returned the last evaluated expression. However, it’s good practice to use explicit return() statements, especially for complex functions:

gc_content = function(sequence) {
  seq_upper = toupper(sequence)
  gc_count = str_count(seq_upper, "[GC]")
  total_bases = str_count(seq_upper, "[ATGC]")
  gc_proportion = gc_count / total_bases

  return(gc_proportion)  # Explicit return
}




What if we want to return more than one piece of information? Use a list or data frame:

gc_content_detailed = function(sequence) {
  seq_upper = toupper(sequence)

  # Count each base
  a_count = str_count(seq_upper, "A")
  t_count = str_count(seq_upper, "T")
  g_count = str_count(seq_upper, "G")
  c_count = str_count(seq_upper, "C")

  total = a_count + t_count + g_count + c_count
  gc_prop = (g_count + c_count) / total

  # Return as a data frame
  result = tibble(
    sequence = sequence,
    length = total,
    A = a_count,
    T = t_count,
    G = g_count,
    C = c_count,
    gc_content = round(gc_prop, 4)
  )

  return(result)
}

gc_content_detailed("ATGCGATCGATCGATCG")

# A tibble: 1 × 7
  sequence          length     A     T     G     C gc_content
  <chr>              <int> <int> <int> <int> <int>      <dbl>
1 ATGCGATCGATCGATCG     17     4     4     5     4      0.529





You can specify default values for arguments. This is useful when most calls will use the same value:

gc_content = function(sequence, digits = 4) {
  seq_upper = toupper(sequence)
  gc_count = str_count(seq_upper, "[GC]")
  total_bases = str_count(seq_upper, "[ATGC]")
  gc_proportion = gc_count / total_bases

  return(round(gc_proportion, digits))
}

gc_content("ATGCGATCGATCG")       # Uses default 4 digits

[1] 0.5385

gc_content("ATGCGATCGATCG", 2)    # Override to 2 digits

[1] 0.54






An important concept to understand is that functions operate in their own environment. Objects created inside a function don’t appear in your global environment:

test_function = function(x) {
  internal_var = x * 2  # This stays inside the function
  return(internal_var)
}

result = test_function(5)
result

[1] 10

# Try to access internal_var - it doesn't exist in the global environment
# internal_var  # Would produce an error

This is called lexical scoping. R looks for objects in this order:

Inside the function
In the environment where the function was defined
In parent environments, up to the global environment







Important



Functions are “sandboxed” — they don’t pollute your global environment with intermediate variables. This makes code cleaner and reduces the risk of naming conflicts.







Control flow allows your functions to behave differently based on conditions:

# Calculate enzyme velocity using Michaelis-Menten kinetics
enzyme_velocity = function(substrate, vmax, km, inhibitor = NULL, ki = NULL) {

  if (is.null(inhibitor)) {
    # No inhibitor: standard Michaelis-Menten
    velocity = (vmax * substrate) / (km + substrate)
  } else {
    # Competitive inhibition
    if (is.null(ki)) {
      stop("If inhibitor concentration is provided, ki must also be specified")
    }
    apparent_km = km * (1 + inhibitor / ki)
    velocity = (vmax * substrate) / (apparent_km + substrate)
  }

  return(velocity)
}

# Test without inhibitor
enzyme_velocity(substrate = 10, vmax = 100, km = 5)

[1] 66.66667

# Test with inhibitor
enzyme_velocity(substrate = 10, vmax = 100, km = 5, inhibitor = 2, ki = 3)

[1] 54.54545





When you have many conditions, nested if/else statements become hard to read. Use dplyr::case_when() instead:

# Classify gene expression fold changes
classify_expression = function(fold_change) {
  category = case_when(
    fold_change >= 2 ~ "strongly_upregulated",
    fold_change >= 1.5 ~ "upregulated",
    fold_change <= 0.5 ~ "strongly_downregulated",
    fold_change <= 0.67 ~ "downregulated",
    TRUE ~ "unchanged"
  )
  return(category)
}

# Test with a vector of fold changes
fold_changes = c(0.3, 0.6, 1.0, 1.6, 2.5)
classify_expression(fold_changes)

[1] "strongly_downregulated" "downregulated"          "unchanged"             
[4] "upregulated"            "strongly_upregulated"  


The equivalent data.table::fcase() function works similarly:

classify_expression_dt = function(fold_change) {
  fcase(
    fold_change >= 2, "strongly_upregulated",
    fold_change >= 1.5, "upregulated",
    fold_change <= 0.5, "strongly_downregulated",
    fold_change <= 0.67, "downregulated",
    default = "unchanged"
  )
}

classify_expression_dt(fold_changes)

[1] "strongly_downregulated" "downregulated"          "unchanged"             
[4] "upregulated"            "strongly_upregulated"  








You’ll often need to apply the same operation to many inputs. The traditional approach uses for loops (?@sec-r-for-loops):

# Calculate GC content for multiple sequences
sequences = c("ATGCGATCG", "GGGGCCCC", "AAAATTTT", "ATATATAT")

# Using a for loop
gc_results = NULL
for (i in 1:length(sequences)) {
  gc_results[i] = gc_content(sequences[i])
}
gc_results

[1] 0.5556 1.0000 0.0000 0.0000


This works, but has several problems:

Verbose: Lots of boilerplate code
Error-prone: Easy to make off-by-one errors
Pollutes environment: The loop variable i persists after the loop
Not R-like: R is designed for vectorized operations




The functional programming approach treats iteration as applying a function across elements:

# Much cleaner!
gc_results = lapply(sequences, gc_content)
gc_results

[[1]]
[1] 0.5556

[[2]]
[1] 1

[[3]]
[1] 0

[[4]]
[1] 0


The result is a list. To get a vector instead:

gc_results = sapply(sequences, gc_content)
gc_results

ATGCGATCG  GGGGCCCC  AAAATTTT  ATATATAT 
   0.5556    1.0000    0.0000    0.0000 


To combine results into a data frame, use our detailed function with bind_rows():

lapply(sequences, gc_content_detailed) %>%
  bind_rows()

# A tibble: 4 × 7
  sequence  length     A     T     G     C gc_content
  <chr>      <int> <int> <int> <int> <int>      <dbl>
1 ATGCGATCG      9     2     2     3     2      0.556
2 GGGGCCCC       8     0     0     4     4      1    
3 AAAATTTT       8     4     4     0     0      0    
4 ATATATAT       8     4     4     0     0      0    





The purrr package provides a consistent and powerful set of mapping functions (base R’s apply() family, ?@sec-apply-family, plays the same role):

# map() returns a list (like lapply)
map(sequences, gc_content)

[[1]]
[1] 0.5556

[[2]]
[1] 1

[[3]]
[1] 0

[[4]]
[1] 0

# map_dbl() returns a numeric vector
map_dbl(sequences, gc_content)

[1] 0.5556 1.0000 0.0000 0.0000

# map_df() returns a data frame
map_df(sequences, gc_content_detailed)

# A tibble: 4 × 7
  sequence  length     A     T     G     C gc_content
  <chr>      <int> <int> <int> <int> <int>      <dbl>
1 ATGCGATCG      9     2     2     3     2      0.556
2 GGGGCCCC       8     0     0     4     4      1    
3 AAAATTTT       8     4     4     0     0      0    
4 ATATATAT       8     4     4     0     0      0    





For complex analyses, separate the function definition from iteration:

# Define a function for processing protein sequences
analyze_protein = function(sequence) {
  seq_upper = toupper(sequence)
  length = nchar(seq_upper)

  # Count hydrophobic residues (simplified)
  hydrophobic = str_count(seq_upper, "[AILMFVPW]")

  # Count charged residues
  charged = str_count(seq_upper, "[DEKRH]")

  tibble(
    sequence = sequence,
    length = length,
    hydrophobic_pct = round(hydrophobic / length * 100, 1),
    charged_pct = round(charged / length * 100, 1)
  )
}

# Some sample protein sequences
proteins = c(
  "MKTAYIAKQRQISFVKSHFSRQLEERLGLIEVQAPILSRVGDGTQDNLSGAEKAVQVKVKALPDAQFEVVHSLAKWKRQQIAAALEHHHHHH",
  "MVLSPADKTNVKAAWGKVGAHAGEYGAEALERMFLSFPTTKTYFPHFDLSH",
  "GLSDGEWQQVLNVWGKVEADIAGHGQEVLIRLFTGHPETLEKFDKFKHLKTEAEMKASEDLKKHGTVVLTALGGILKKKGHHEAELKPLAQSHATKHKIPIKYLEFISDAIIHVLHSKHPGDFGADAQGAMTKALELFRNDIAAKYKELGFQG"
)

# Apply to all proteins
map_df(proteins, analyze_protein)

# A tibble: 3 × 4
  sequence                                    length hydrophobic_pct charged_pct
  <chr>                                        <int>           <dbl>       <dbl>
1 MKTAYIAKQRQISFVKSHFSRQLEERLGLIEVQAPILSRVGD…     92            42.4        32.6
2 MVLSPADKTNVKAAWGKVGAHAGEYGAEALERMFLSFPTTKT…     51            47.1        25.5
3 GLSDGEWQQVLNVWGKVEADIAGHGQEVLIRLFTGHPETLEK…    153            41.2        34.6






Sometimes you need to iterate over multiple inputs simultaneously.



# Simulate growth curves with different parameters
simulate_growth = function(time, k, n0, carrying_capacity) {
  # Logistic growth model
  n = carrying_capacity / (1 + ((carrying_capacity - n0) / n0) * exp(-k * time))

  tibble(
    time = time,
    k = k,
    n0 = n0,
    K = carrying_capacity,
    population = round(n, 0)
  )
}

# Parameters for different bacterial strains
params = tibble(
  k = c(0.5, 0.8, 0.3),              # Growth rates
  n0 = c(100, 50, 200),              # Initial populations
  carrying_capacity = c(10000, 15000, 8000)  # Carrying capacities
)

# Run simulations for each strain at time = 10
pmap_df(params, ~simulate_growth(time = 10, k = ..1, n0 = ..2, carrying_capacity = ..3))

# A tibble: 3 × 5
   time     k    n0     K population
  <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>      <dbl>
1    10   0.5   100 10000       5999
2    10   0.8    50 15000      13633
3    10   0.3   200  8000       2720





A cleaner approach for complex cases is to pass a data frame of input combinations (Figure 1 shows the result):

# Create all parameter combinations
simulation_params = expand.grid(
  time = seq(0, 20, by = 2),
  strain = c("wild_type", "mutant_A", "mutant_B")
) %>%
  as_tibble() %>%
  mutate(
    k = case_when(
      strain == "wild_type" ~ 0.5,
      strain == "mutant_A" ~ 0.8,
      strain == "mutant_B" ~ 0.3
    ),
    n0 = 100,
    carrying_capacity = 10000
  )

# Function that takes a row of parameters
run_simulation = function(row_data) {
  simulate_growth(
    time = row_data$time,
    k = row_data$k,
    n0 = row_data$n0,
    carrying_capacity = row_data$carrying_capacity
  ) %>%
    mutate(strain = row_data$strain)
}

# Run all simulations
results = map_df(1:nrow(simulation_params), function(i) {
  run_simulation(simulation_params[i, ])
})

# Plot the results
ggplot(results, aes(x = time, y = population, color = strain)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    title = "Bacterial Growth Curves",
    x = "Time (hours)",
    y = "Population Size",
    color = "Strain"
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma)







Figure 1: Simulated bacterial growth curves for three strains, produced by mapping a function over a data frame of parameter combinations












# Good names
calculate_gc_content()
normalize_expression()
fit_growth_curve()

# Bad names
func1()
do_stuff()
f()




Add comments explaining what the function does, its arguments, and return value:

# Calculate the melting temperature of a DNA primer
#
# Uses the Wallace rule for short oligonucleotides (<14 bp)
# or the nearest-neighbor method for longer sequences
#
# Arguments:
#   sequence: DNA sequence (string of A, T, G, C)
#   method: "wallace" or "nearest_neighbor"
#
# Returns:
#   Melting temperature in degrees Celsius

calculate_tm = function(sequence, method = "wallace") {
  seq_upper = toupper(sequence)
  length = nchar(seq_upper)

  a_count = str_count(seq_upper, "A")
  t_count = str_count(seq_upper, "T")
  g_count = str_count(seq_upper, "G")
  c_count = str_count(seq_upper, "C")

  if (method == "wallace" || length < 14) {
    # Wallace rule: Tm = 2(A+T) + 4(G+C)
    tm = 2 * (a_count + t_count) + 4 * (g_count + c_count)
  } else {
    # Simplified nearest-neighbor approximation
    tm = 64.9 + 41 * (g_count + c_count - 16.4) / length
  }

  return(tm)
}

calculate_tm("ATGCGATCGATCG")

[1] 40





Check that inputs are valid before processing:

gc_content_safe = function(sequence) {
  # Check input type
  if (!is.character(sequence)) {
    stop("Sequence must be a character string")
  }

  # Check for valid DNA characters
  seq_upper = toupper(sequence)
  invalid_chars = str_remove_all(seq_upper, "[ATGCN]")
  if (nchar(invalid_chars) > 0) {
    warning(paste("Invalid characters removed:", invalid_chars))
  }

  gc_count = str_count(seq_upper, "[GC]")
  total_bases = str_count(seq_upper, "[ATGC]")

  if (total_bases == 0) {
    stop("No valid DNA bases found in sequence")
  }

  return(gc_count / total_bases)
}

gc_content_safe("ATGCGATCG")     # Works fine

[1] 0.5555556

gc_content_safe("ATGCXYZGATCG")  # Warning about invalid characters

Warning in gc_content_safe("ATGCXYZGATCG"): Invalid characters removed: XYZ


[1] 0.5555556





Each function should do one thing well. Break complex operations into smaller functions:

# Instead of one giant function, break it up:

# Step 1: Clean the sequence
clean_sequence = function(seq) {
  seq %>%
    toupper() %>%
    str_remove_all("[^ATGC]")
}

# Step 2: Calculate base composition
base_composition = function(seq) {
  tibble(
    A = str_count(seq, "A"),
    T = str_count(seq, "T"),
    G = str_count(seq, "G"),
    C = str_count(seq, "C")
  )
}

# Step 3: Derive statistics
sequence_stats = function(composition) {
  total = sum(composition)
  composition %>%
    mutate(
      total = total,
      gc_content = (G + C) / total,
      at_content = (A + T) / total
    )
}

# Combine them in a pipeline
"atgcGATCgatcgNNNN" %>%
  clean_sequence() %>%
  base_composition() %>%
  sequence_stats()

# A tibble: 1 × 7
      A     T     G     C total gc_content at_content
  <int> <int> <int> <int> <int>      <dbl>      <dbl>
1     3     3     4     3    13      0.538      0.462






Writing functions is a fundamental programming skill that will dramatically improve your data analysis workflows:

Basic syntax: function_name = function(args) { body; return(value) }
Return values: Use explicit return() statements; return lists or data frames for multiple values
Default arguments: Provide sensible defaults for commonly-used parameter values
Lexical scoping: Functions operate in their own environment, keeping your global environment clean
Control flow: Use if/else and case_when() to handle different conditions
Functional programming: Prefer lapply()/map() over for loops for iteration
Multiple inputs: Use pmap() or data frame inputs for complex parameter combinations

The next chapter (?@sec-parallel-computing) will show you how to run functions in parallel, catch errors gracefully (?@sec-parallel-errors), and cache results for expensive computations (?@sec-caching).






Tip

Exercise 2: Function with Multiple Returns

  gc = gc_content(sequences[i])

  } else {

title: Writing Functions in R
text:
Throughout this book, we’ve used many functions: some from base R [@rproject2024] (like mean() and sum()), others from packages (like dplyr::filter() and ggplot2::ggplot()) [@wickham2019tidyverse]. But the real power of programming comes from writing your own functions. (?@sec-writing-simple-functions gave a first taste; here we go further.)
Functions allow you to avoid repetition by writing code once and using it many times. When you find yourself copying and pasting the same block of code with minor changes, that’s a sign you should write a function. This also reduces errors—if you find a bug, you fix it in one place rather than tracking down every copy. Functions improve readability by letting you give meaningful names to complex operations; calculate_gc_content(sequence) is far clearer than the five lines of code it might contain. And functions make it easy to share code with colleagues or package your solutions for the broader community.
In biosciences, you’ll often need custom functions for domain-specific tasks: calculating enzyme kinetics parameters, normalizing gene expression data, computing population genetics statistics, or processing experimental replicates according to your lab’s specific protocols.

title: Writing Functions in R
text:
All R functions follow the same basic syntax:
function_name = function(ARGUMENTS) {
  OPERATIONS
  return(VALUE)
}
Let’s break this down:

function_name: A descriptive name for your function
ARGUMENTS: Input values the function accepts
OPERATIONS: What the function does
return(VALUE): What the function gives back

For short functions, you can write everything on one line:
my_short_func = function(x) x^2






Tip



Give your functions short, descriptive names that indicate what they do. calculate_gc_content is better than func1 or cgc.

title: Writing Functions in R
text:
Let’s write a function that calculates the GC content of a DNA sequence — the proportion of guanine (G) and cytosine (C) bases. (The same function is written in Python in ?@sec-py-functions.)

gc_content = function(sequence) {
  # Convert to uppercase for consistency
  seq_upper = toupper(sequence)

  # Count G and C bases
  gc_count = str_count(seq_upper, "[GC]")

  # Calculate total length (excluding any non-ATGC characters)
  total_bases = str_count(seq_upper, "[ATGC]")

  # Return GC proportion
  gc_count / total_bases
}

Test it:

gc_content("ATGCGATCGATCG")

[1] 0.5384615

gc_content("atgcGATCgatcg")  # Works with mixed case

[1] 0.5384615

gc_content("AAAAAATTTTTT")   # Low GC content

[1] 0

gc_content("GGGGGGCCCCCC")   # High GC content

[1] 1




In the example above, R automatically returned the last evaluated expression. However, it’s good practice to use explicit return() statements, especially for complex functions:

gc_content = function(sequence) {
  seq_upper = toupper(sequence)
  gc_count = str_count(seq_upper, "[GC]")
  total_bases = str_count(seq_upper, "[ATGC]")
  gc_proportion = gc_count / total_bases

  return(gc_proportion)  # Explicit return
}




What if we want to return more than one piece of information? Use a list or data frame:

gc_content_detailed = function(sequence) {
  seq_upper = toupper(sequence)

  # Count each base
  a_count = str_count(seq_upper, "A")
  t_count = str_count(seq_upper, "T")
  g_count = str_count(seq_upper, "G")
  c_count = str_count(seq_upper, "C")

  total = a_count + t_count + g_count + c_count
  gc_prop = (g_count + c_count) / total

  # Return as a data frame
  result = tibble(
    sequence = sequence,
    length = total,
    A = a_count,
    T = t_count,
    G = g_count,
    C = c_count,
    gc_content = round(gc_prop, 4)
  )

  return(result)
}

gc_content_detailed("ATGCGATCGATCGATCG")

# A tibble: 1 × 7
  sequence          length     A     T     G     C gc_content
  <chr>              <int> <int> <int> <int> <int>      <dbl>
1 ATGCGATCGATCGATCG     17     4     4     5     4      0.529





You can specify default values for arguments. This is useful when most calls will use the same value:

gc_content = function(sequence, digits = 4) {
  seq_upper = toupper(sequence)
  gc_count = str_count(seq_upper, "[GC]")
  total_bases = str_count(seq_upper, "[ATGC]")
  gc_proportion = gc_count / total_bases

  return(round(gc_proportion, digits))
}

gc_content("ATGCGATCGATCG")       # Uses default 4 digits

[1] 0.5385

gc_content("ATGCGATCGATCG", 2)    # Override to 2 digits

[1] 0.54

title: Writing Functions in R
text:
An important concept to understand is that functions operate in their own environment. Objects created inside a function don’t appear in your global environment:

test_function = function(x) {
  internal_var = x * 2  # This stays inside the function
  return(internal_var)
}

result = test_function(5)
result

[1] 10

# Try to access internal_var - it doesn't exist in the global environment
# internal_var  # Would produce an error

This is called lexical scoping. R looks for objects in this order:

Inside the function
In the environment where the function was defined
In parent environments, up to the global environment







Important



Functions are “sandboxed” — they don’t pollute your global environment with intermediate variables. This makes code cleaner and reduces the risk of naming conflicts.

title: Writing Functions in R
Writing Functions in R
text:
You’ll often need to apply the same operation to many inputs. The traditional approach uses for loops (?@sec-r-for-loops):

# Calculate GC content for multiple sequences
sequences = c("ATGCGATCG", "GGGGCCCC", "AAAATTTT", "ATATATAT")

# Using a for loop
gc_results = NULL
for (i in 1:length(sequences)) {
  gc_results[i] = gc_content(sequences[i])
}
gc_results

[1] 0.5556 1.0000 0.0000 0.0000


This works, but has several problems:

Verbose: Lots of boilerplate code
Error-prone: Easy to make off-by-one errors
Pollutes environment: The loop variable i persists after the loop
Not R-like: R is designed for vectorized operations




The functional programming approach treats iteration as applying a function across elements:

# Much cleaner!
gc_results = lapply(sequences, gc_content)
gc_results

[[1]]
[1] 0.5556

[[2]]
[1] 1

[[3]]
[1] 0

[[4]]
[1] 0


The result is a list. To get a vector instead:

gc_results = sapply(sequences, gc_content)
gc_results

ATGCGATCG  GGGGCCCC  AAAATTTT  ATATATAT 
   0.5556    1.0000    0.0000    0.0000 


To combine results into a data frame, use our detailed function with bind_rows():

lapply(sequences, gc_content_detailed) %>%
  bind_rows()

# A tibble: 4 × 7
  sequence  length     A     T     G     C gc_content
  <chr>      <int> <int> <int> <int> <int>      <dbl>
1 ATGCGATCG      9     2     2     3     2      0.556
2 GGGGCCCC       8     0     0     4     4      1    
3 AAAATTTT       8     4     4     0     0      0    
4 ATATATAT       8     4     4     0     0      0    





The purrr package provides a consistent and powerful set of mapping functions (base R’s apply() family, ?@sec-apply-family, plays the same role):

# map() returns a list (like lapply)
map(sequences, gc_content)

[[1]]
[1] 0.5556

[[2]]
[1] 1

[[3]]
[1] 0

[[4]]
[1] 0

# map_dbl() returns a numeric vector
map_dbl(sequences, gc_content)

[1] 0.5556 1.0000 0.0000 0.0000

# map_df() returns a data frame
map_df(sequences, gc_content_detailed)

# A tibble: 4 × 7
  sequence  length     A     T     G     C gc_content
  <chr>      <int> <int> <int> <int> <int>      <dbl>
1 ATGCGATCG      9     2     2     3     2      0.556
2 GGGGCCCC       8     0     0     4     4      1    
3 AAAATTTT       8     4     4     0     0      0    
4 ATATATAT       8     4     4     0     0      0    





For complex analyses, separate the function definition from iteration:

# Define a function for processing protein sequences
analyze_protein = function(sequence) {
  seq_upper = toupper(sequence)
  length = nchar(seq_upper)

  # Count hydrophobic residues (simplified)
  hydrophobic = str_count(seq_upper, "[AILMFVPW]")

  # Count charged residues
  charged = str_count(seq_upper, "[DEKRH]")

  tibble(
    sequence = sequence,
    length = length,
    hydrophobic_pct = round(hydrophobic / length * 100, 1),
    charged_pct = round(charged / length * 100, 1)
  )
}

# Some sample protein sequences
proteins = c(
  "MKTAYIAKQRQISFVKSHFSRQLEERLGLIEVQAPILSRVGDGTQDNLSGAEKAVQVKVKALPDAQFEVVHSLAKWKRQQIAAALEHHHHHH",
  "MVLSPADKTNVKAAWGKVGAHAGEYGAEALERMFLSFPTTKTYFPHFDLSH",
  "GLSDGEWQQVLNVWGKVEADIAGHGQEVLIRLFTGHPETLEKFDKFKHLKTEAEMKASEDLKKHGTVVLTALGGILKKKGHHEAELKPLAQSHATKHKIPIKYLEFISDAIIHVLHSKHPGDFGADAQGAMTKALELFRNDIAAKYKELGFQG"
)

# Apply to all proteins
map_df(proteins, analyze_protein)

# A tibble: 3 × 4
  sequence                                    length hydrophobic_pct charged_pct
  <chr>                                        <int>           <dbl>       <dbl>
1 MKTAYIAKQRQISFVKSHFSRQLEERLGLIEVQAPILSRVGD…     92            42.4        32.6
2 MVLSPADKTNVKAAWGKVGAHAGEYGAEALERMFLSFPTTKT…     51            47.1        25.5
3 GLSDGEWQQVLNVWGKVEADIAGHGQEVLIRLFTGHPETLEK…    153            41.2        34.6

title: Writing Functions in R
text:
Sometimes you need to iterate over multiple inputs simultaneously.



# Simulate growth curves with different parameters
simulate_growth = function(time, k, n0, carrying_capacity) {
  # Logistic growth model
  n = carrying_capacity / (1 + ((carrying_capacity - n0) / n0) * exp(-k * time))

  tibble(
    time = time,
    k = k,
    n0 = n0,
    K = carrying_capacity,
    population = round(n, 0)
  )
}

# Parameters for different bacterial strains
params = tibble(
  k = c(0.5, 0.8, 0.3),              # Growth rates
  n0 = c(100, 50, 200),              # Initial populations
  carrying_capacity = c(10000, 15000, 8000)  # Carrying capacities
)

# Run simulations for each strain at time = 10
pmap_df(params, ~simulate_growth(time = 10, k = ..1, n0 = ..2, carrying_capacity = ..3))

# A tibble: 3 × 5
   time     k    n0     K population
  <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>      <dbl>
1    10   0.5   100 10000       5999
2    10   0.8    50 15000      13633
3    10   0.3   200  8000       2720





A cleaner approach for complex cases is to pass a data frame of input combinations (Figure 1 shows the result):

# Create all parameter combinations
simulation_params = expand.grid(
  time = seq(0, 20, by = 2),
  strain = c("wild_type", "mutant_A", "mutant_B")
) %>%
  as_tibble() %>%
  mutate(
    k = case_when(
      strain == "wild_type" ~ 0.5,
      strain == "mutant_A" ~ 0.8,
      strain == "mutant_B" ~ 0.3
    ),
    n0 = 100,
    carrying_capacity = 10000
  )

# Function that takes a row of parameters
run_simulation = function(row_data) {
  simulate_growth(
    time = row_data$time,
    k = row_data$k,
    n0 = row_data$n0,
    carrying_capacity = row_data$carrying_capacity
  ) %>%
    mutate(strain = row_data$strain)
}

# Run all simulations
results = map_df(1:nrow(simulation_params), function(i) {
  run_simulation(simulation_params[i, ])
})

# Plot the results
ggplot(results, aes(x = time, y = population, color = strain)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    title = "Bacterial Growth Curves",
    x = "Time (hours)",
    y = "Population Size",
    color = "Strain"
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma)







Figure 1: Simulated bacterial growth curves for three strains, produced by mapping a function over a data frame of parameter combinations

title: Writing Functions in R
text:
# Good names
calculate_gc_content()
normalize_expression()
fit_growth_curve()

# Bad names
func1()
do_stuff()
f()




Add comments explaining what the function does, its arguments, and return value:

# Calculate the melting temperature of a DNA primer
#
# Uses the Wallace rule for short oligonucleotides (<14 bp)
# or the nearest-neighbor method for longer sequences
#
# Arguments:
#   sequence: DNA sequence (string of A, T, G, C)
#   method: "wallace" or "nearest_neighbor"
#
# Returns:
#   Melting temperature in degrees Celsius

calculate_tm = function(sequence, method = "wallace") {
  seq_upper = toupper(sequence)
  length = nchar(seq_upper)

  a_count = str_count(seq_upper, "A")
  t_count = str_count(seq_upper, "T")
  g_count = str_count(seq_upper, "G")
  c_count = str_count(seq_upper, "C")

  if (method == "wallace" || length < 14) {
    # Wallace rule: Tm = 2(A+T) + 4(G+C)
    tm = 2 * (a_count + t_count) + 4 * (g_count + c_count)
  } else {
    # Simplified nearest-neighbor approximation
    tm = 64.9 + 41 * (g_count + c_count - 16.4) / length
  }

  return(tm)
}

calculate_tm("ATGCGATCGATCG")

[1] 40





Check that inputs are valid before processing:

gc_content_safe = function(sequence) {
  # Check input type
  if (!is.character(sequence)) {
    stop("Sequence must be a character string")
  }

  # Check for valid DNA characters
  seq_upper = toupper(sequence)
  invalid_chars = str_remove_all(seq_upper, "[ATGCN]")
  if (nchar(invalid_chars) > 0) {
    warning(paste("Invalid characters removed:", invalid_chars))
  }

  gc_count = str_count(seq_upper, "[GC]")
  total_bases = str_count(seq_upper, "[ATGC]")

  if (total_bases == 0) {
    stop("No valid DNA bases found in sequence")
  }

  return(gc_count / total_bases)
}

gc_content_safe("ATGCGATCG")     # Works fine

[1] 0.5555556

gc_content_safe("ATGCXYZGATCG")  # Warning about invalid characters

Warning in gc_content_safe("ATGCXYZGATCG"): Invalid characters removed: XYZ


[1] 0.5555556





Each function should do one thing well. Break complex operations into smaller functions:

# Instead of one giant function, break it up:

# Step 1: Clean the sequence
clean_sequence = function(seq) {
  seq %>%
    toupper() %>%
    str_remove_all("[^ATGC]")
}

# Step 2: Calculate base composition
base_composition = function(seq) {
  tibble(
    A = str_count(seq, "A"),
    T = str_count(seq, "T"),
    G = str_count(seq, "G"),
    C = str_count(seq, "C")
  )
}

# Step 3: Derive statistics
sequence_stats = function(composition) {
  total = sum(composition)
  composition %>%
    mutate(
      total = total,
      gc_content = (G + C) / total,
      at_content = (A + T) / total
    )
}

# Combine them in a pipeline
"atgcGATCgatcgNNNN" %>%
  clean_sequence() %>%
  base_composition() %>%
  sequence_stats()

# A tibble: 1 × 7
      A     T     G     C total gc_content at_content
  <int> <int> <int> <int> <int>      <dbl>      <dbl>
1     3     3     4     3    13      0.538      0.462
